items.title: bash 沙箱：研究 --unshare-user / --unshare-pid
items.body:
## 背景

`bash` 工具的 bubblewrap 沙箱（#76）目前只做文件系统隔离：`--ro-bind / /` + 可写目录白名单。没有使用 `--unshare-user` / `--unshare-pid`。

## 问题

1. **`--unshare-user`（user namespace）**：bwrap 默认在无 userns 的环境会失败（或自动降级）；显式 unshare 可确保沙箱内的进程无法提权（与 codex 的做法一致：`args.push("--unshare-user")` + `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` + seccomp）。
2. **`--unshare-pid`（PID namespace）**：沙箱内进程看到独立的 PID 空间（bwrap 成为 1 号进程），但会**影响我们现有的进程管理**：
   - `bash.py` 用 `start_new_session=True` + `os.killpg(SIGKILL)` 杀整个进程组——unshare-pid 后 bwrap 的子进程是否仍在同一进程组、killpg 能否穿透 PID namespace，需要验证；
   - `Agent.interrupt()` 依赖 `on_proc` 持有的 Popen 句柄杀进程，行为需要重测；
   - 沙箱内 `ps`/`kill` 语义变化，可能影响需要跨进程协作的命令。

## 待研究

- [ ] 验证 `--unshare-user --unshare-pid` 下 killpg / interrupt / timeout 行为
- [ ] 是否需要配合 seccomp / `no_new_privs`
- [ ] 对 `run_in_background` 等场景的影响
- [ ] 与 codex（`codex-rs/linux-sandbox`）的参数对齐：`--new-session --unshare-user --unshare-pid --proc /proc`

## 参考

- dsh：沙箱只约束文件效果，不承诺进程可见性
- codex：`create_bwrap_flags_full_filesystem` 恒加 `--unshare-user --unshare-pid`

items.title: Dev box without unprivileged user namespaces: grant them to unshare with an AppArmor profile
items.body:
One of our dev boxes runs Ubuntu 26.04 with `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`. There, `unshare --user --map-root-user` fails with:

```
unshare: write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted
```

`fractal-runtime`'s `process::tests::inherited_outer_procfs_refuses_launch_and_control_before_mutation` re-runs itself under `unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork`. So on that box it failed on plain main every time, and `st-test`'s `linux-gate` could not sign there. The other dev box (NixOS) and the CI boxes allow unprivileged user namespaces, and the test passes on them.

The interim fix (the linked PR) skips that one test outside CI when `unshare` itself is refused, and records the skip in the evidence note as `env_skips`.

**Way out (needs root on that dev box):** grant user namespaces to `unshare` alone with an AppArmor profile. Inside `nix develop` on that box, `unshare` resolves to `/usr/bin/unshare`. This is Ubuntu's documented approach, which leaves the sysctl and every other program restricted:

```
# /etc/apparmor.d/unshare-userns
abi <abi/4.0>,
include <tunables/global>

profile unshare-userns /usr/bin/unshare flags=(unconfined) {
  userns,
}
```

Load it with `apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/unshare-userns`. Check it with `unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork true` as the build user, which should exit 0. Once that passes, the test runs there again, notes on that box show `env_skips=none`, and the skip can be removed.

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop window never appears on a bare-metal host: renderers crash on /dev/shm (ENOSTAT 3) — Chromium userns sandbox cannot remount /proc

labels.name: desktop/shell
labels.description: The desktop app's window and OS integration: window chrome, title bar, tray, dock, menus, keyboard s

items.body:
**Related:** [#138277](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/138277) reports the same crash family (Chromium renderer fails on `/dev/shm` inside the out-of-process sandbox, "Try `sudo chmod 1777 /dev/shm`"), but with errno **2 (ENOENT, "No such file or directory")**. This report is errno **3 (ENOSTAT, "No such process")** with a specific, reproducible root cause on a **bare-metal** host, so it is filed separately and cross-references #138277.

### Bug Description
Hermes Desktop launches but **no window ever appears**. Every Chromium **renderer** child process crashes within the first fraction of a second with a `/dev/shm` shared-memory error (errno 3 = `ENOSTAT`). The window-drawing renderers all die, so nothing shows. (GPU/utility children can survive; in the broken run the GPU child also failed to launch and the zygote reported errors, but the window-killer is the renderer `/dev/shm` crash.) The same app runs fine on a normal host.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. On a host where **unprivileged processes cannot remount `/proc` inside a (user-namespace) mount namespace** — confirmed here by:
   - `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount true` -> `rc=0` (user-ns + mount-ns works)
   - `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --mount-proc true` -> `unshare: mount /proc failed: Operation not permitted` (fails)
2. Make sure the desktop is launched with the sandbox **enabled** (i.e. `desktop.electron_flags` in `config.yaml` does *not* include `--no-sandbox`; remove the workaround if present).
3. Run `hermes desktop`.
4. Observe: no window; the process tree repeatedly spawns and crashes Chromium `--type=renderer` processes.

### Expected Behavior
The window opens and the desktop app is usable.

### Actual Behavior
No window appears. Each renderer dies immediately with (repeated for every renderer):
```
Creating shared memory in /dev/shm/.org.chromium.Chromium.xfrdMX failed: No such process (3)
Unable to access(W_OK|X_OK) /dev/shm: No such process (3)
FATAL: ... This is frequently caused by incorrect permissions on /dev/shm.  Try 'sudo chmod 1777 /dev/shm' to fix.
Renderer process crashed
```

### Affected Component
Other — Hermes Desktop (Electron/Chromium renderer process). The Desktop app is not listed among the dropdown options.

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)
N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report
No public paste uploaded (the config carries a live API token). Relevant evidence is inline below.

### Operating System
Linux Mint 22.3, kernel `7.0.0-38-generic`, x86_64, **bare metal** (Gigabyte motherboard; `systemd-detect-virt` -> `none`; *not* a KVM/VM host). AppArmor is not running, the launcher has **no** seccomp filter, and kernel lockdown mode is off.

### Python Version
3.14.9

### Hermes Version
Hermes Agent v0.22.5 (2026.9.24) · stable · local bf0203a794a0 (Electron/Chromium 44.9.3)

### Additional Logs / Traceback
`/dev/shm` is healthy and writable in the normal namespace (tmpfs, mode `1777`, ~32 GB). The failure is in the renderer's *sandbox* mount namespace. Precise, measured behavior on this bare-metal host:
```
unshare --mount true                                  -> Operation not permitted
unshare --user --map-root-user true                   -> OK
unshare --user --map-root-user --mount true           -> OK
                                                      (user-ns + mount-ns: 30 mounts, healthy /dev/shm tmpfs present)
unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --mount-proc true
                                                      -> mount /proc failed: Operation not permitted
unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --ipc --uts --pid --net --mount true -> OK
```

### Root Cause Analysis (observation only — not a fix)
Chromium's out-of-process **user-namespace** sandbox must, after creating a user namespace and a mount namespace, **remount `/proc`** (to reflect the remapped UIDs). On this host that remount is denied for unprivileged processes (`mount /proc failed: Operation not permitted`), while the user-namespace + mount-namespace *without* the `/proc` remount works and contains a healthy `/dev/shm`. The net effect is that the sandbox's mount-namespace setup is left broken/incomplete, and each renderer dies on its very first shared-memory allocation to `/dev/shm` with `ENOSTAT (3, "No such process")`. (The exact kernel setting/bug denying the `/proc` remount on this particular kernel is not identified; it is *not* an LSM — AppArmor is off and the launcher has no seccomp filter — so it likely needs a kernel-side confirmation from the team.)

Compounding the problem: the desktop launcher's "userns sandbox available?" probe only tests **user-namespace** creation (`unshare --user --map-root-user`), which succeeds here, so it concludes the sandbox is usable and does **not** add `--no-sandbox`. The renderers are therefore spawned into a broken sandbox and crash.

Workaround (verified, **not a fix**; no PR offered in this report): launch the desktop with the renderer sandbox disabled, e.g. in `config.yaml`:
```yaml
desktop:
  electron_flags:
    - --no-sandbox
    - --disable-dev-shm-usage
```
With these flags the renderers run in the normal namespace where `/dev/shm` is present, and the window opens and stays up (confirmed: main process and renderers remain alive for minutes, no new crashes).

### Proposed Fix
(Left blank — no fix offered in this report.)

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?
- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: uac-r2: /unshare-user last-reader rule has no round-76 'Restricted wins' carve-out
items.body:
Found by task 174's verifier (PR #1481, pass 1). Pre-existing.

`/unshare-user` enforces S5 (never remove the last internal reader) with no exception for round 76 ("Restricted wins over the last-reader rule"). On a secure **Restricted** record, an operator therefore cannot remove an external-flagged user who is the last reader. Only the automatic `RestrictedExternalShareRemover` does that, and for a child of a Restricted parent only on routed visits (#1478).

**Fix:** in `/unshare-user`, allow removing an external-flagged last reader on a Restricted record (effective value), as the remover does. Add tests for both the allowed and the refused case.

items.title: util-linux: restore exec securebits after unshare/nsenter enter a user namespace
items.body:
## What

Adds `05-exec-aware-userns.patch` to the util-linux 2.42 series so that `unshare` and `nsenter` set the exec securebits again after creating or joining a user namespace. Closes #32.

## Why

The kernel resets a process's securebits to 0 when it creates or joins a user namespace, and that includes the locked bits. So `unshare --user -- python -c ...` ran without `EXEC_DENY_INTERACTIVE`, even under `setpriv --securebits +exec_deny_interactive,+exec_deny_interactive_locked`. I confirmed this on Linux 7.3.0: the bits read 0 after `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)`, and an unprivileged process can set them again.

## How

- Two new helpers in `lib/caputils.c`, which both tools already link: `get_exec_securebits()` saves `EXEC_RESTRICT_FILE`, `EXEC_DENY_INTERACTIVE`, and their locks. `restore_exec_securebits()` sets them again. If that fails it prints a warning and carries on, the same way exec-aware programs carry on when the securebits are unavailable.
- `unshare` calls them around `unshare()`.
- `nsenter` calls them around both `setns()` passes, before it changes UID/GID or forks.
- The `unshare(1)` and `nsenter(1)` man pages each get a note under `--user`.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Only the exec bits are restored.** Restoring `NOROOT` and the other bits would change what root can do in the new namespace, for example caps under `unshare -r`, so they stay as the kernel sets them.
- **No `CAP_SETPCAP` needed.** The kernel lets unprivileged processes set the exec bits, so the restore works whether or not the process has capabilities in the target namespace.
- If no exec bits were set, the helpers make no `PR_SET_SECUREBITS` call, so nothing changes for normal use or on kernels older than 6.14.

## Testing

- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.util-linux-exec-aware` passes all 13 cases. The new ones lock both exec bits and check `unshare --user`, `unshare --map-root-user`, and `nsenter --user --preserve-credentials` against a child in its own user namespace. They print SKIP if user namespaces aren't available. The `--map-root-user` case also prints SKIP, with the errno, if writing `uid_map` is denied. Ubuntu 24.04's AppArmor userns restriction does that on the GitHub runners.
- Run against stock util-linux 2.42.4, the three new cases fail.
- The four existing patches export byte-identical from the stgit stack the new patch was made in.
- `nix fmt` and `reuse lint` pass.
- I did not run the full `nix flake check` or build on aarch64-linux.

items.title: Allow unsharing user from a group
Keep the Windows VM mount boundary test's mounts off the host when run as root

labels.name: verified
labels.description: Omarchy Triage has verified that this issue is ready for final review

items.body:
## Summary

`test/shell.d/windows-vm-mount-boundary-test.sh` only entered a private namespace when it started unprivileged. Run as root (`sudo ./test/shell`, a root CI container), it skipped that step and mounted tmpfs straight over the host's live `/run`, `/var` and `/home`, then left them mounted. This is the "missing /home, /var/lib, /var/log, /run" incident from #9834: the directories were hidden under those mounts, not deleted.

```diff
-if ((EUID != 0)); then
-  unshare --user --map-root-user --mount ... bash "$0"   # non-root only
-fi
+if not already in the test's private namespace
+  root:     exec unshare --mount --propagation private bash "$0"
+  non-root: exec unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --propagation private bash "$0"
+  no namespace available: skip
+if this mount namespace is still PID 1's
+  fail before mounting anything
```

The second check fails closed if the re-exec is ever bypassed.

## Evidence

Disposable privileged Arch Linux ARM container, counting `/run`, `/var`, `/home` mounts and entries in `/var/lib`:

- **Before** (quattro defbf90e, as root): test passes, then `mounts=3`, `/var/lib` 4 → 1 entries; `run-test`, `var-test` and `home-parent` tmpfs left on `/run`, `/var`, `/home`.
  **After** (as root): 11 ok, `mounts=0`, `/var/lib` still 4 entries.
- Root with the re-exec bypassed: `not ok - refusing to mount over /run, /var and /home in the host's mount namespace`, nothing mounted.
- Non-root: unchanged, all ok.
- Unprivileged container (no `unshare --mount`): `# SKIP`, exit 0.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

Test-only change; nothing shipped to users changes.

**Blast Radius:** tests

Root runs of this one test now need `unshare --mount` and skip where it is unavailable, instead of mounting over the host.

Replaces #9834, which refused root for the whole suite and missed this test.

items.title: Fix bwrap profil
items.body:
## Description

1. Install a targeted AppArmor profile at plugin setup (setup.py)

Adds a plugin setup hook that, on Ubuntu-like systems where the restriction is actually active, installs an AppArmor profile granting the userns capability to the bwrap binary only (/etc/apparmor.d/bwrap) and loads it with apparmor_parser. This is scoped to bwrap rather than globally disabling the sysctl. The hook:
- no-ops on non-Linux, non-Ubuntu-like systems, and when the restriction isn't active;
- is idempotent — skips if the profile is already present;
- degrades gracefully, printing manual instructions if sudo/apparmor_parser aren't available.

2. Fix the sandbox support pre-check (common/sandbox/bwrap.py)

_check_bwrap_support() probed support with bwrap --unshare-user --version, but bwrap handles --version during argument parsing and exits before ever unsharing — so the probe passed even when user namespaces were blocked. The pre-check therefore reported "supported" and the real failure surfaced only mid-run as raw bwrap stderr.

The probe now actually creates a user namespace (bwrap --unshare-user --ro-bind / / true), forcing bwrap through the uid-map setup that AppArmor blocks. It correctly returns unsupported (with the AppArmor message) when restricted, and succeeds once the profile is installed.

3. Offer to repair in place when the sandbox is unsupported (common/mixins.py)

With the pre-check now accurate, _ensure_sandbox_supported() catches the AppArmor case before launch. Instead of only printing shell commands for the user to copy, it offers to run the plugin setup right there (installing the profile, prompting for sudo as needed), then re-checks support and continues the command if the fix worked. The offer is only shown when the restriction is the actual blocker (restriction active and bwrap installed); otherwise the original error-and-abort behavior is preserved.

items.title: Linux process-ownership cleanup fails when /proc/<pid>/environ is unreadable across user namespaces (EACCES)
items.body:
## Environment

- rea-agents 6.7.0, Linux (Fedora 44 kernel 7.2.9, inside a rootless podman/distrobox container)
- Ghidra 12.1.4 + Temurin JRE 21
- MCP mode (`rea mcp`)

## Summary

`open_binary` (Ghidra provider) fails with `cleanup_incomplete` because REA's POSIX process-ownership verification reads `/proc/<pid>/environ` of *every* live process and treats `EACCES` as a hard failure. In environments with bwrap-sandboxed processes in separate user namespaces (browsers, image loaders, desktop portals), those processes' `environ` is mode `0400` owned by the same uid yet returns `EACCES` across the namespace boundary. REA classifies them as strict failures instead of withheld/unverified, so Ghidra cleanup never succeeds even though the analysis itself completed.

## Reproduction

1. Have any bwrap (or other user-namespace) process running as the same uid.
2. `rea mcp` → `open_binary` on any ELF.
3. Result: `cleanup_incomplete`, `reason: process ownership token could not be read for N live process(es): environment_errno_EACCES=N`, with candidate PIDs that are unrelated bwrap processes.

## Evidence

- `/proc/<pid>/environ` mode `0400`, owner == current uid, but `open()` returns `EACCES` (errno 13) for bwrap processes in other user namespaces.
- Running REA under `unshare --user --pid --fork --mount-proc` (private PID namespace) makes `open_binary` succeed end-to-end, confirming the cause is the process-table scan, not Ghidra/Java.

## Suggested fix

In `ProcessOwnership` / `scanTokenOwnedProcesses`, treat an `EACCES` (and `EPERM`) failure reading `/proc/<pid>/environ` as "environment withheld from inspection" (i.e. unverified) when the process is not a descendant of the REA launcher and not in a sampled/owned process group — mirroring the existing Darwin `environmentWithheldFromInspection` handling. Alternatively, scope the cleanup scan to the REA process's own PID namespace / descendants rather than the global process table.

## Workaround used

Launch `rea mcp` under `unshare --user --pid --fork --mount-proc` so its process table contains only its own processes.

items.title: [Bubblewrap] Sandboxed workloads can create user namespaces; add --disable-userns or a seccomp filter

labels.name: OS-Linux
labels.description: Applies specifically to Linux hosts or Linux behavior.

labels.name: Backend-LXC
labels.description: Linux container isolation implemented with LXC.

labels.name: Backend-Bubblewrap
labels.description: Linux process isolation implemented with Bubblewrap.

items.body:
## Relevant area(s)

Linux, Bubblewrap backend.

## Description

Code inside a Bubblewrap sandbox can create new user namespaces, and MXC 1.0 has no option to prevent it. On a host that allows unprivileged user namespaces, a workload can run `unshare -Ur` and become uid 0 in a namespace of its own, or start a nested `bwrap`. That exposes the kernel's user-namespace attack surface (namespaced capabilities, mounts, netfilter) to untrusted code, which is often the larger part of a container escape.

This matters most when MXC runs inside a container. Docker needs a relaxed seccomp profile for bwrap to start at all, and then every sandboxed workload inherits the ability to create namespaces too, even though only the supervisor needs it.

## Steps to reproduce

With mxc-sdk 1.0.0 on Linux (bubblewrap 0.12, unprivileged user namespaces enabled), run `unshare -Ur id` in a sandbox with the default request (no network access):

```rust
let out = v1::run(ContainerRequest::new("unshare -Ur id"), Default::default()).unwrap();
// Exited(0), stdout: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),65534
```

## Expected

An option, ideally the default, that prevents the workload from creating user namespaces. bubblewrap supports this with `--disable-userns` (since 0.8), which requires `--unshare-user`.

## Actual

`bwrap_command.rs` builds the namespace arguments without `--disable-userns`. In proxy mode the sandbox joins the supervisor's user namespace instead of unsharing one (`uses_external_userns`), so `--disable-userns` cannot be used there, and a seccomp filter blocking `unshare`/`clone` with `CLONE_NEWUSER` (passed with `--seccomp`) would be needed instead.

## Suggested change

- Pass `--disable-userns` whenever MXC uses `--unshare-user`.
- For proxy mode, add a small seccomp filter that denies `CLONE_NEWUSER` for the workload.
- Expose it in the request (for example a `process.allowUserNamespaces` setting, default false) for workloads that genuinely need nested sandboxes.

For context: we currently work around this with a `bwrap` wrapper on `PATH` that adds such a filter, which depends on MXC's exact bwrap arguments and breaks on upgrade.

items.title: Sandbox: a sandboxed command can create a nested user namespace; disable it
items.body:
## Context

Found while drafting ADR-012 (#284, PR #285), measured on bubblewrap 0.11.2 and Linux 6.18: under the sandbox's current bubblewrap flags, a process inside the sandbox (an operator tool or a declarative command tool) can create a nested user namespace and become uid 0 inside it. That grants no host privilege by itself, but it hands the sandboxed code the kernel attack surface of unprivileged user namespaces, a recurring source of local privilege escalations. bubblewrap's `--disable-userns` (which requires an explicit `--unshare-user`) closes it.

## Scope

- Add `--unshare-user` and `--disable-userns` to the bwrap argv built in `src/agents_system/connectors/operator.py`, for operator tools and declarative command tools alike. Fail closed with a clear error when the installed bubblewrap is too old to support it; document the minimum version.
- A regression test, gated on `bwrap`: a sandboxed command that tries to create a user namespace (for example `unshare -U true`, or Python's `os.unshare(os.CLONE_NEWUSER)`) fails, while the existing allowed commands still run.
- Add the case to the mechanism suite's sandbox checks.
- Docs EN + ES (`docs/operations/sandbox-bwrap.md`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A nested user namespace cannot be created inside the sandbox (test).
- [ ] The existing sandbox, command-tool and `commands` capability tests still pass.
- [ ] Live: the mechanism suite, `tests/test_live_eval_capabilities.py -k commands` and `tests/test_live_eval_guardrails.py` on the reference model.

items.title: Deny user namespaces to apps in both modes (seccomp installed by the spawn gate)
items.body:
Apps can create user namespaces in both deployment modes, and an unprivileged user namespace is the usual first step of a kernel privilege escalation.

Measured 2026-09-30 / 10-01 on Ubuntu 26.04 microVMs (`unshare --user --map-root-user id -u` from inside an app):

| mode | result |
| --- | --- |
| root creekd (default sandbox: own PID ns, NoNewPrivs, per-app UID, `Seccomp: 0`) | **exit 0, uid 0 inside** |
| shipped unit (`RestrictNamespaces=true`) | `Operation not permitted` |

So the shipped unit blocks it only because systemd's filter applies to creekd's children; a root creekd (the documented production setup with `Delegate=yes`) does not. Whether the kernel allows it otherwise is distro-dependent (Ubuntu's stock kernel restricts it via AppArmor; Debian, Fedora, Arch do not).

Proposal: the spawn gate installs a seccomp filter before exec that denies `unshare`/`clone`/`clone3` with `CLONE_NEWUSER` (and probably the other `CLONE_NEW*` flags apps have no business using), returning `EPERM`. `clone3` takes its flags in a struct seccomp cannot inspect, so it is denied with `ENOSYS` to make libc fall back to `clone` — the approach systemd uses. Opt-out per app for workloads that need namespaces.

Acceptance: an app under a root creekd gets `EPERM` from `unshare --user`; ordinary runtimes (Bun, Node, Go) still start and serve; documented in DESIGN.md's isolation model.

items.body:
## Summary

On the fork pool (rbe-fork, instance `oss-fork`) `//cmd/bd:bd_managed_local_test` fails in 0.2s before any Go test starts:

```
==================== Test output for //cmd/bd:bd_managed_local_test:
unshare: unshare failed: No space left on device
```

`tools/bazel/go_test_offline.sh` execs `unshare --user --map-root-user --net`; ENOSPC from `unshare(2)` is the namespace-limit errno ("the limit on the nesting depth or number of namespaces would be exceeded"), not disk. The script's header says this is the designed fail-closed for a host that does not allow unprivileged user namespaces.

## Evidence

items.title: apply-seccomp fails with EPERM on /proc/self/setgroups on bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04: bwrap 0.9.0 clears CapBnd before the helper nests its own userns
items.body:
## Summary

On a bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04 host with unprivileged user namespaces fully enabled, every sandboxed command fails with:

```
apply-seccomp: write /proc/self/setgroups (nested userns is capability-restricted; caller must provide CAP_SYS_ADMIN): Permission denied
```

The cause is not an AppArmor restriction (#74) and not a container capability set (#417). It is that `bwrap` 0.9.0 — the newest version Ubuntu 24.04 ships — clears the **capability bounding set** to zero for the process it spawns. Since `apply-seccomp` runs *inside* `bwrap` and then tries to create its own nested user namespace, it can never regain `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, so the `/proc/self/setgroups` write is unconditionally denied.

Dropping the optional seccomp helper makes the sandbox work immediately, which confirms the ordering is the problem rather than the host configuration.

## Environment

- `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`: 0.0.67 (also reproduced on 0.0.42)
- Claude Code: 2.1.220 (native installer), Node v24.14.0
- Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-136-generic, x86_64
- `bubblewrap`: 0.9.0-1ubuntu0.1 (the only candidate in the noble archive)
- Bare metal, not a container: `/proc/1/cgroup` is `0::/init.scope`, no `/.dockerenv`
- Host userns is unrestricted:
  - `kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone = 1`
  - `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 0`
  - `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined = 0`
  - `/proc/self/attr/current` is `unconfined`, AppArmor `bwrap` profile installed anyway
  - `unshare --user --map-root-user echo ok` succeeds
  - `bwrap --dev-bind / / --unshare-user echo ok` succeeds

## Reproduction

```sh
srt /bin/echo ok
# apply-seccomp: write /proc/self/setgroups (nested userns is capability-restricted; ...): Permission denied
```

`srt --debug` shows the ordering:

```
[SeccompFilter] Found apply-seccomp binary: .../vendor/seccomp/x64/apply-seccomp (x64)
[Sandbox Linux] Applying seccomp filter for Unix socket blocking
[Sandbox Linux] Wrapped command with bwrap (network, filesystem, seccomp(unix-block) restrictions)
```

## Root cause evidence

The helper works standalone, and fails under `bwrap` regardless of which namespace flags `bwrap` is given:

```sh
HELPER=.../@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime/vendor/seccomp/x64/apply-seccomp

$HELPER /bin/echo ok                                     # ok
unshare --user --map-root-user $HELPER /bin/echo ok      # ok

bwrap --dev-bind / / $HELPER /bin/echo ok                # EPERM on setgroups
bwrap --dev-bind / / --unshare-user $HELPER /bin/echo ok # EPERM on setgroups
bwrap --dev-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-pid $HELPER /bin/echo ok  # EPERM
bwrap --dev-bind / / --cap-add ALL $HELPER /bin/echo ok  # EPERM
```

The process state inside `bwrap` explains it:

```sh
bwrap --dev-bind / / sh -c 'grep -E "NoNewPrivs|CapEff|CapBnd" /proc/self/status'
# CapEff:  0000000000000000
# CapBnd:  0000000000000000     <-- bounding set cleared
# NoNewPrivs: 1
```

With an empty bounding set, a nested `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)` cannot grant `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, so neither `uid_map` nor `setgroups` can be written:

```sh
bwrap --dev-bind / / unshare --user --map-root-user echo ok
# unshare: write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted
```

Note that `bwrap --cap-add ALL` restores `CapBnd` to `000001ffffffffff` for the immediate child, but the helper still fails, since the capabilities are dropped again across the `execve` of an unprivileged uid.

## Workaround

Removing the optional helper resolves it, at the cost of Unix-socket blocking:

```sh
mv .../vendor/seccomp/x64/apply-seccomp{,.disabled}
srt /bin/echo ok
# ok
```

## Suggestion

Either apply the seccomp filter *outside* `bwrap` — the helper succeeds when it owns the outer namespace, as the `unshare --user` case above shows — or have the filter reuse the user namespace `bwrap` already created instead of nesting a second one. Failing that, detecting an empty `CapBnd` and degrading to the no-seccomp path with a warning would be better than a hard failure, since the enclosing `bwrap` still provides filesystem and network isolation.

Related but distinct: #74 (AppArmor userns restriction, not applicable here) and #417 (container without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, fails on `uid_map` rather than `setgroups`).

items.body:
Part 4 of 7 of the Genkit in a Box stack. Depends on #6460.

## What

OS sandboxes for `execRunner`'s `isolate:` option.

```ts
// seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux; throws elsewhere (e.g. Windows)
box(ai, { runner: execRunner({ self: true, isolate: localSandbox() }) });

bubblewrap({ roBind: ['/path/to/repo'], tmpfs: ['/tmp'] });
sandboxExec({ profile: '(version 1)\n(deny default)\n(allow network* (local ip))' });
```

**These are dev-time guardrails, not containment.** The README has the full table.
- **`sandboxExec()` (macOS)** blocks filesystem writes outside `/tmp`. Reads are open.
- **`bubblewrap()` (Linux)** only mounts a read-only system plus a tmpfs `/tmp`. Home, repo and credentials aren't present.
- **Both** leave network egress open (the box has to reach the reflection host) and set no resource limits.
- **Hostile code** belongs in the container runner (next PR).

Split out from #6460 so the sandbox profiles can be reviewed on their own.

Both providers pass the spawn env through untouched, so `execRunner`'s `inheritEnv`/`env` apply inside the sandbox too (tested end to end through `sandbox-exec`).

### Testapp
`src/index.ts` now uses `isolate: localSandbox()`. The README walks through what each platform blocks, for example `echo hi > ~/nope.txt` failing on macOS while `/tmp` works.

## Testing
`providers_test.ts` covers the spawn transforms per platform. I also checked by hand on macOS: a boxed write to `$HOME` fails with "Operation not permitted" and a write to `/tmp` succeeds.

items.title: Running the test suite logs out the desktop session (SIGTERM/SIGKILL to every user process)
items.body:
Running `pytest` on a Linux desktop terminates the whole user session. On GNOME that's an instant logout. It happened to me twice, and anyone running the suite outside a sandbox will hit it.

**Cause:** `tests/test_bg_tool_gates.py::test_bg_release_kills_and_snaps_output` gives `_acp_terminal_release` a fake process with `pid = 1`, and the release path calls the real `os.killpg`:

```
_acp_terminal_release → _terminal_close → _kill_terminal_proc
  → os.killpg(1, SIGTERM)
  → os.killpg(1, SIGKILL)   # escalation in terminal.py
```

glibc implements `killpg(g)` as `kill(-g)`, so pgid 1 is `kill(-1)`: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, to **every process the user owns**. The journal shows `ssh-agent`, `gnome-keyring-daemon`, Xwayland and D-Bus all receiving signal 15 at the same instant, followed by session teardown.

**Reproduce safely** (a PID namespace contains `kill(-1)`):

```
unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --mount-proc \
  python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_bg_tool_gates.py -k bg_release_kills
```

**Fix:** #1. `bridge/acp/terminal.py` refuses `killpg` on pgid ≤ 1 and falls back to `proc.terminate()`/`kill()`; real terminal children always have a pgid > 1. The test mocks `os.killpg`, and `conftest.py` makes any test that signals pid ≤ 1 fail loudly instead.

**Until then:** don't run the suite directly on a desktop; wrap it in the `unshare` line above.

items.title: claude plugin eval: every Bash call fails with "bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR" (ref #14719, #55585)
items.body:
### Preflight Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing issues. This is the error from #14719 and #55585, both closed as not planned by the inactivity bot and now locked, so I am filing a new one as they ask. The new part is where it hits: `claude plugin eval`.
- [x] This is a single bug report
- [x] I am using the latest version of Claude Code

### What's Wrong?

In `claude plugin eval` runs with `--allow-tools Bash`, every Bash tool call made by the agent under test fails immediately with:

```
bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted
```

This includes trivial commands (`echo hi`, `pwd`, `node --version`). It happened in 6 of 6 runs across two eval cases. Glob, Grep and Read work, so agents fall back to reading files and still produce plausible answers. Graders that check the reply or a `tool_used: Bash` call still pass, which hides the failure unless you read the trace.

### What Should Happen?

Bash should run in eval runs, or the runner should fail the run with a clear sandbox error instead of letting the agent continue without a shell.

### Error Messages/Logs

From `--keep-temp` traces (`/tmp/claude-eval-*/out/trace.jsonl`):

```
Bash: node <plugin>/skills/.../check.mjs spec.md
  > Exit code 1 | bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted
Bash: which node; node --version
  > Exit code 1 | bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted
Bash: echo hello
  > Exit code 1 | bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted
```

### Steps to Reproduce

1. In a plugin repo with an `evals/` suite, pick any case whose agent uses Bash.
2. Run:
   ```
   claude plugin eval . --trust-plugin --scaffold --allow-tools Bash --ablation none --keep-temp --case '<case>' --json /tmp/out.json
   ```
3. Open `/tmp/claude-eval-*/out/trace.jsonl`: every Bash `tool_result` is the error above.

### Environment

- Claude Code 2.1.270 (native install)
- Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, kernel 7.0.0-34-generic
- bubblewrap 0.9.0 (`/usr/bin/bwrap`, not setuid)
- `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 1`, `kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone = 1`
- AppArmor profiles present: `unprivileged_userns`, `lxc-usernsexec`; no profile for `bwrap`

### What I checked

- On the host, all of these exit 0:
  - `bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-net true`
  - `bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-net true`
  - nested: `bwrap --dev-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-net -- bwrap --dev-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-net true`
- In a normal interactive Claude Code session on the same machine, Bash works, but the process has no PID namespace (`NSpid` shows a single PID). That looks like the silent sandbox fallback described in #55585. The eval runner does not fall back: it keeps sandboxing each command, and each one fails.

So I cannot reproduce the failure with plain `bwrap`. It seems specific to the bwrap invocation Claude Code uses, and in the eval runner nothing falls back when it fails.

### Related

#14719, #55585

items.title: Sandbox: make the host's toolchains (dotnet, node, java, …) available to sandboxed commands
items.body:
## Problem

Sandboxed shell commands only see a small slice of the host. `Sandbox.#run` (apps/runner/src/sandbox.ts) mounts:
- `/usr`, `/lib` and `/lib64`, read-only;
- `/bin` → `usr/bin`;
- the session's own home and worktree.

It runs commands with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin` and **no `/etc`**, apart from the CA bundle written by `trust-store.ts`.

So a toolchain works only if it happens to live entirely under `/usr` and needs nothing from `/etc`. Common setups fail in a sandbox even though they work on the host:

| Toolchain install | Where it lives | In the sandbox today |
|---|---|---|
| apt `nodejs`, `dotnet-sdk-8.0` (Ubuntu feed), `golang`, `python3` | `/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib/...` | ✓ works |
| Debian alternatives (`java`, `javac`, sometimes `node`/`python`) | `/usr/bin/java` → `/etc/alternatives/java` → … | ✗ dangling symlink (no `/etc`) |
| Anything in `/usr/local/bin` (manual installs, `pip install --user`, some installers) | `/usr/local/bin` | ✗ not on PATH (visible only by full path) |
| nvm / fnm / volta, `~/.dotnet` (dotnet-install.sh), rustup, pyenv, sdkman | the host user's home | ✗ the host home isn't mounted |
| `/opt/...` (JDKs, Microsoft dotnet tarballs, vendor SDKs), Linuxbrew `/home/linuxbrew` | outside `/usr` | ✗ not mounted |
| Tools that read `/etc` (e.g. `/etc/dotnet/install_location`, `/etc/java-*`, `/etc/npmrc`) | `/etc` | ✗ |

Today the only workaround is the unsandboxed `host_bash` path: each command needs the host owner's approval and runs with the host's own network and credentials. That defeats the purpose for routine `dotnet build` / `npm test` runs.

## Goal

Host owners can let sandboxed sessions use the toolchains already installed on the host, such as `dotnet`, `node`/`npm`, `java`, `go`, `cargo` and `python`. The sandbox's guarantees stay the same:
- no host credentials or private files reach the sandbox;
- toolchains are mounted read-only;
- the only network is the egress proxy;
- the existing resource limits apply.

## Proposed design (for discussion)

**1. A host-side allowlist of tool directories, chosen by the host owner.** For example `pistead connect --sandbox-tool /opt/dotnet --sandbox-tool ~/.nvm/versions/node/v24.11.0`, or the desktop app's host settings. Each entry:
- is mounted read-only at the same path (`--ro-bind`), so absolute paths, RPATHs and symlinks keep working;
- puts its `bin/`, or the directory itself, on the sandbox's `PATH` after `/usr/bin`.

Paths are validated:
- absolute and canonical (`realpath`);
- not `/`, `/etc`, `/home`, the host home itself, or the runner's data and cache directories;
- not containing likely secrets (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.config`, `.npmrc`, `.docker`, `.kube`, `.git-credentials`, …).

Mounting `~/.nvm/versions/node/vX` is fine; mounting `~` is not.

**2. `/usr/local` on PATH.** It's already mounted (as part of `/usr`). Adding `/usr/local/bin` to the sandbox `PATH`, behind the same opt-in or by default, is a one-line change that covers many manual installs.

**3. A curated read-only `/etc` subset.** Make `/etc/alternatives` and specific tool directories (`/etc/java-*`, `/etc/dotnet`) available, read-only. Never all of `/etc`: `passwd`, `shadow`, host network configuration and credential files stay out. Open question: should this be a fixed list, or follow from the chosen tools (resolve each tool's symlink chain and mount what it passes through)?

**4. Detect and advertise.** The connector reports which tools a sandboxed session can run (name and version, e.g. `dotnet 8.0.4`, `node 24.11.0`). It does this by running `--version` inside the sandbox at startup, not on the host, so the result is honest. The tools are shown on the host in Settings → Hosts and listed in the agent's instructions ("This host provides: dotnet 8.0.4 (/opt/dotnet), node 24.11.0 …"). That way the agent stops trying tools that aren't there.

**5. Per-session writable state, never the host's.** Toolchains write caches and config under HOME. They should go to the session's home, which is already private and per-session, never to the host user's:
- `DOTNET_CLI_HOME`, `NUGET_PACKAGES`;
- `npm_config_cache`, `COREPACK_HOME`;
- `GOPATH`, `GOMODCACHE`, `CARGO_HOME`, `GRADLE_USER_HOME`.

Point them there, with `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1`, `DOTNET_NOLOGO=1` and similar, and keep the backup size budget in mind (caches can be large; consider excluding them from backups). Package downloads already go through the egress proxy, and the network policy's package-registry allowlist already includes npm, NuGet, PyPI, crates.io, Maven and Go.

**6. Workspace / session control.** Tools are a host property, but a workspace may want to require some. Open question: is a host-level allowlist enough, or should the session-creation UI show which tools a host offers?

## Security considerations

- Everything is mounted read-only, so a session can't change the host's toolchain for other sessions or for the host user.
- Mounting user-home subdirectories risks exposing files beside the toolchain. Validate paths, refuse ones that contain dotfiles with known secrets, and document that the owner is choosing what to share.
- Binaries run inside the existing namespace, cgroup and seccomp limits, so no new privilege is involved. setuid binaries stay ineffective (`--unshare-user`, `--cap-drop ALL`).
- macOS and Windows hosts aren't sandboxed this way today. This issue is about the Linux bwrap sandbox.

## Acceptance

- On a host with dotnet installed in `/opt/dotnet` (or `~/.dotnet`) and node via nvm, the owner adds both, and a sandboxed session can run `dotnet build` and `npm ci && npm test` on a cloned repository. Packages are fetched through the egress proxy, and nothing is written outside the session's directories.
- `java` from Debian's alternatives works in the sandbox.
- Tools that weren't added stay invisible; a path containing `.ssh` or similar is refused with a reason.
- The agent's instructions and the host's settings list the available tools and their versions.
- Tests cover the mount and PATH assembly, path validation, and tool detection run inside the sandbox.

items.title: Container hardening: untrusted plugins/browser run with SYS_ADMIN, root, seccomp and AppArmor unconfined
items.body:
Untrusted code (community plugins fetched from arbitrary GitHub repositories, and Chromium rendering hostile pages) runs inside a container with near-privileged settings.

**Configuration** ([compose.yaml](https://github.com/NikGro/argus-osint/blob/0e3ca1977452032e081400802d04379e7bb7a0fd/compose.yaml))
- `user: "0:0"`, overriding the Dockerfile's `USER workbench`
- `cap_add: [SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW, SETUID, SETGID, CHOWN, KILL]`
- `security_opt: [seccomp:unconfined, apparmor:unconfined]`
- `/dev/net/tun`

**Isolation in place**
- [core/worker_broker.py](https://github.com/NikGro/argus-osint/blob/0e3ca1977452032e081400802d04379e7bb7a0fd/core/worker_broker.py#L109-L128): `unshare --mount --net --pid`
- [core/worker_entry.py](https://github.com/NikGro/argus-osint/blob/0e3ca1977452032e081400802d04379e7bb7a0fd/core/worker_entry.py#L46-L72): setuid to a random UID, `no_new_privs`, rlimits
- No user namespace and no seccomp filter.

**Why this matters**
With seccomp unconfined, plugin code has the full syscall surface (for example `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)`, `io_uring`, `keyctl`) that Docker's default profile blocks. A kernel privilege escalation from a worker lands as root with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` and no AppArmor, which is a well-known container-escape position. Plugin installation is open to any `https://github.com/owner/repo` ([plugin_manager.py](https://github.com/NikGro/argus-osint/blob/0e3ca1977452032e081400802d04379e7bb7a0fd/plugin_manager.py#L398-L416)).

This is a defense-in-depth gap. No exploit was attempted.

**Suggested fix**
- Split the privileged VPN gateway and broker into their own container. Run plugins and the browser in a container with default seccomp and AppArmor, no added capabilities, and a non-root user.
- Alternatively, apply a seccomp profile and a user namespace (`unshare --user --map-root-user`, or bubblewrap/nsjail) to workers.

items.title: Stop user namespace probes from hanging the shell suite
items.body:
Where user namespaces are refused, `./test/shell` never finishes. Three files skip as intended (`windows-vm-mount-boundary-test.sh`, `remove-dev-env-sudo-security-test.sh`, and the cross-UID probe in `update-stay-awake-security-test.sh`), and then the runner stays on `tee` for good. We measured this in an Arch container on Docker Desktop under Docker's default seccomp profile, where `unshare --user` fails with "Operation not permitted": each of the three held the run until the leftover process was killed by hand, after 4, 4 and 9.5 minutes.

The cause is in util-linux `unshare` (read in 2.42.4, the same on master). With `--map-users`, `--map-groups` or `--map-auto` it forks a helper to write the mappings before calling unshare(2), and the helper waits on an eventfd for the parent to report that the call succeeded. When the call fails, the parent exits through `err()` without telling it, so the helper stays blocked, reparented to init, with the test's stdout still open. The test file exits, but the pipe to `tee` never reaches EOF. `--map-root-user` and `--map-current-user` on their own write the mappings without a helper and fail cleanly, which is why the other namespace tests in the suite are unaffected.

This adds `user_namespace_available` to `base-test.sh`. It runs `unshare --user --mount true`: the same unshare(2) flags the three probes use, without mappings, so nothing is forked. The probes ask it before trying a mapping form. Where user namespaces work it succeeds and the probes run exactly as before. Only `test/` and `docs/` change.

The new `user-namespace-probe-test.sh` puts a stub `unshare` first in `PATH` that fails every call and, for the mapping forms, leaves a process holding stdout the way util-linux does. It reads the Windows VM boundary probe through a pipe under `timeout`, which kills the whole process group if the pipe stays open, so a regression fails the file instead of hanging it. It also fails any test that passes `--map-users`, `--map-groups` or `--map-auto` without calling the helper. `docs/testing.md` gets a bullet next to the existing note on inherited output pipes.

This touches the same probe line in `windows-vm-mount-boundary-test.sh` as #11768, which changes the root path there. Whichever lands second needs a one-line rebase, and the unprivileged `--map-auto` branch that #11768 keeps still needs the guard.

Validation: in the same container, `user-namespace-probe-test.sh` fails on `quattro` (its 10 s `timeout` fires) and passes with this change. Breaking each new assertion on its own (the probe exiting non-zero, reporting a pass instead of a skip, the helper call removed from `remove-dev-env-sudo-security-test.sh` or from `update-stay-awake-security-test.sh`) makes the file fail at that assertion. items.title: feat(charters): tell gate and builder seats how to get a test database inside Boundaries 2
items.body:
## What happened

In one taoq-ai/taoqi cloud session, about ten gate and builder seats each needed Postgres for the DB-backed suites. No charter says how to get one. Each seat worked it out alone, with these results:
- The scratch root `/tmp/claude-0` is mode 700, so the `postgres` user cannot reach a cluster under the seat's scratch folder. Seats used `unshare --user --map-user=<postgres uid>` or setpriv. One seat put its cluster in `/tmp/q2pg-g2`, outside Boundaries 2.
- `initdb` defaults to SQL_ASCII, which breaks SQLAlchemy/psycopg. Seats had to discover `-E UTF8 --locale=C.UTF-8`.
- The scratch path is too long for a Unix socket, so seats needed `unix_socket_directories=''` and TCP.
- Postgres roles are cluster-wide, so two seats on one cluster raced on the role reset and got false setup errors. Two seats picked the same port.
- Some gates gave up and marked the DB suites unmeasured, relying on CI.

## Expected

A short, tested recipe in the gate and builder charters (or a `wuwei` helper): a private cluster per seat under its scratch folder, with UTF8, TCP on a port derived from the seat and item, and a teardown. Or a documented rule that DB-backed probes rest on CI when the sandbox cannot run a cluster.

Related: #309 (seat sandboxing).

items.title: linux: an absent write-denied file reads as empty, not "Permission denied"
items.body:
## What

On Linux, a write deny on a file that does not exist yet is covered by an **empty read-only regular file** instead of `/dev/null`.

## Why

bubblewrap gives every `--ro-bind` the `nodev` mount flag, and opening a device node on a `nodev` mount fails with `EACCES`. So the `/dev/null` cover over an absent protected file did not read as empty: it refused to open.

The visible symptom is a login shell. `~/.bash_profile` is a mandatory deny; when it does not exist, `bash -l` inside the sandbox prints

```
/bin/bash: /home/<user>/.bash_profile: Permission denied
```

and, having failed on `.bash_profile`, never reads `~/.profile` (so `~/.local/bin` is missing from `PATH`, the umask is not set, and so on). Any tool that reads a protected file it has yet to create (`.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, `.mcp.json` …) got the same refusal instead of an empty file.

Reproduction without the library, with bubblewrap 0.9.0:

```
$ H=$(mktemp -d)
$ bwrap --unshare-user --dev-bind / / --ro-bind /dev/null "$H/.bash_profile" --setenv HOME "$H" /bin/bash -l -c 'echo ok'
/bin/bash: /tmp/tmp.XXXX/.bash_profile: Permission denied
ok
$ : > "$H/empty"; chmod 0400 "$H/empty"
$ bwrap --unshare-user --dev-bind / / --ro-bind "$H/empty" "$H/.bash_profile" --setenv HOME "$H" /bin/bash -l -c 'echo ok; echo x > "$HOME/.bash_profile"'
ok
/bin/bash: line 1: /tmp/tmp.XXXX/.bash_profile: Read-only file system
```

## How

- `ensureEmptyFileSource()` is the file twin of `ensureEmptyMountSourceDir()`: one read-only empty file of our own (`<tmpdir>/claude-empty-XXXXXX/empty`, dir `0700`, file `0400`), made on first use, revalidated with `lstat` before reuse, removed by `cleanupBwrapMountPoints()` together with the mount points.
- The absent-leaf branch binds that file where it bound `/dev/null`; intermediate components keep the empty directory. The directory that holds the file is pinned read-only inside the sandbox, like the directory source, so a sandboxed command with a writable `$TMPDIR` cannot write through the source to the denied destination.
- Same prefix as the directory source, so tooling and tests that tell a placeholder's source by its name keep working; the directory source's pin stays the last mount.
- Read-deny masks of existing files and the symlink masks still use `/dev/null`: refusing to open is what a read deny means. This change is only about write denies on files that do not exist.

The host mount point bubblewrap makes (an empty `0444` file) is unchanged, so `isStaleBwrapMountPoint`-style detection and the clean-up are as before.

## Tests

- New `test/sandbox/absent-deny-file-reads-empty.test.ts`: the source is a regular empty read-only file of ours, its directory is pinned, one source per wrap and gone with the clean-up; and, with a live bubblewrap, `cat` of the denied absent path reads empty while the write gets `Read-only file system`, and `bash -l` with `HOME` at the cwd starts without `Permission denied`.
- Existing tests that spelled the cover as `--ro-bind /dev/null <path>` now assert the empty-file placeholder (`deny-path-made-meanwhile`, `readonly-deny-dir-binds`, `readonly-deny-dir-stubs`, `linux-unmakeable-mount-point`); `stale-mount-point` counts only empty directories as directory sources.
- `bun test`, `tsc --noEmit` (both configs), `eslint`, `prettier --check`: see the run notes in the PR conversation.

items.title: [Bug]: containers with their own multi-range user namespace fail under rootless Podman (--userns=keep-id)
items.body:
### Bug Description

Rootless Podman runs the OCI runtime as root (uid 0) of a user namespace that it maps with newuidmap/newgidmap from /etc/subuid. That namespace's `/proc/self/setgroups` is `allow`. For `--userns=keep-id`, Podman asks the runtime for a new user namespace with three ranges and `additionalGids: [1000]`. youki fails in two ways:

- **With additionalGids:** validation refuses the spec: `unprivileged user can't set supplementary groups`.
- **Without additionalGids:** the mapping is never written, and the container fails with `EINVAL` from setresgid(0).

crun runs both.

Cause, at eb07b60173fca880e4287d5bc0de2580edec2c91:

1. `utils::rootless_required()` (`crates/libcontainer/src/utils.rs:264`) returns true for any process in a non-initial user namespace, so a root runtime in Podman's namespace counts as unprivileged:
   - `UserNamespaceConfig::privileged` (`crates/libcontainer/src/user_ns.rs:223`);
   - the supplementary-group check in `validate_spec_for_new_user_ns()` (`user_ns.rs:290-311`).
2. Because it is unprivileged, several ranges go to newuidmap/newgidmap (`user_ns.rs:164`, `write_id_mapping()` at `:403`). Run by that namespace's root they are refused: `newuidmap: uid range [0-1000) -> [1-1001) not allowed`.
3. `write_id_mapping()` doesn't check the helper's exit status (`.output()` at `user_ns.rs:441`). The uid_map/gid_map stays empty, and the intermediate process fails later at `set_id(0, 0)` (`container_intermediate_process.rs:122`) with EINVAL.

How the others do it:
- crun (1.30, `src/libcrun/linux.c` `write_id_map()`, lines 4520-4537) runs the helper only when its euid isn't 0. As root it writes the full map to `/proc/<pid>/uid_map` itself.
- runc (v1.4.1, `libcontainer/init_linux.go:491-495`) sets `additionalGids` whenever setgroups isn't `deny`.

Why it is safe: the kernel lets an unprivileged process map a new user namespace only after it writes `deny` to its setgroups (CVE-2014-8989, user_namespaces(7)). A namespace whose setgroups is `allow` was therefore mapped by a privileged writer. Its root may map ids it holds into a child namespace, and may set groups.

A related detail: `set_supplementary_gids()` (`crates/libcontainer/src/process/init/process.rs:822`) returns early when `additionalGids` is empty. The container process then keeps the supplementary groups of whoever started the runtime. runc and crun call setgroups with the empty list.

### Steps to Reproduce

No Podman needed. The user namespace is made with util-linux's `unshare --map-auto`, which uses newuidmap/newgidmap the way Podman does:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# repro.sh <runtime> <groups|nogroups> [workdir]
set -eu
RT=$1; CASE=$2; W=${3:-$(pwd)/work-$RT-$CASE}
here=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
rm -rf "$W"; mkdir -p "$W/bundle/rootfs"
tar -xzf "$here/alpine-minirootfs-3.24.2-x86_64.tar.gz" -C "$W/bundle/rootfs" 2>/dev/null
cd "$W/bundle"
"$RT" spec --rootless
python3 - "$CASE" <<'P'
import json, sys
s = json.load(open('config.json'))
s['process']['terminal'] = False
s['process']['args'] = ['sh', '-c', 'id; cat /proc/self/uid_map']
s['process']['user'] = {'uid': 1000, 'gid': 1000}
if sys.argv[1] == 'groups':
    s['process']['user']['additionalGids'] = [1000]
m = [{'containerID': 0, 'hostID': 1, 'size': 1000},
     {'containerID': 1000, 'hostID': 0, 'size': 1},
     {'containerID': 1001, 'hostID': 1001, 'size': 64536}]
s['linux']['uidMappings'] = m
s['linux']['gidMappings'] = m
json.dump(s, open('config.json', 'w'), indent=2)
P
echo "outer: $(tr -s ' ' < /proc/self/uid_map | tr '\n' ';') setgroups=$(cat /proc/self/setgroups)"
"$RT" --root "$W/state" run --bundle "$W/bundle" "repro-$CASE"
```

1. Put `alpine-minirootfs-3.24.2-x86_64.tar.gz` (sha256 `c5ca053cfe1d85c5b96dff8b9bc57045f7f184a30ffb6b65776409ca90388677`) next to the script. You need an /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid entry for your user.
2. `unshare --user --map-auto --map-root-user ./repro.sh youki groups`:
   ```
   outer:  0 1000 1; 1 100000 65536; setgroups=allow
   ERROR libcontainer::user_ns: user is unprivileged. Supplementary groups cannot be set in a rootless container for this user due to CVE-2014-8989 user=Uid(0)
   ERROR libcontainer::user_ns: failed to validate spec for new user namespace: unprivileged user can't set supplementary groups
   ERROR youki: error in executing command: invalid spec for new user namespace container
   ```
3. `unshare --user --map-auto --map-root-user ./repro.sh youki nogroups`:
   ```
   ERROR libcontainer::syscall::linux: failed to set real, effective and saved set gid err=EINVAL gid=Gid(0)
   ERROR libcontainer::process::container_main_process: failed to run intermediate process EINVAL: Invalid argument
   ERROR youki: error in executing command: failed to create container: intermediate process error EINVAL: Invalid argument
   ```
4. The same two commands with `crun` print `uid=1000 gid=1000 groups=1000` and `uid=1000 gid=1000`, and the three-range uid_map.

The helper refusal can be seen on its own:

```sh
unshare --user --map-auto --map-root-user sh -c 'unshare --user sleep 20 & q=$!; sleep 0.5; newuidmap $q 0 1 1000 1000 0 1 1001 1001 64536; echo rc=$?'
# newuidmap: uid range [0-1000) -> [1-1001) not allowed
# rc=1
```

With Podman: `podman --runtime youki run --rm --userns=keep-id alpine id` fails with `unprivileged user can't set supplementary groups`. The same command with crun prints `uid=1000(emilio) gid=1000(emilio) groups=1000(emilio)`.

### Expectation

As with crun: the container runs with the requested three-range mapping, as uid/gid 1000, with exactly the requested supplementary groups.

### System and Setup Info

```
youki version: 0.7.0
commit: 0.7.0-eb07b60173fca880e4287d5bc0de2580edec2c91
Kernel-Release    7.2.7-1-cachyos
Operating System  CachyOS
Cgroup setup      unified
```

util-linux 2.42.4, Podman 6.1.2, crun 1.30.1.

### Additional Context

The runtime spec (config.md, "User") only says `additionalGids` are group IDs "in the container namespace to be added to the process". It sets no restriction for runtimes that run inside a user namespace.

items.body:
## Context

Follow-up recorded by ADR-079 (#5913 amendment, 2026-07-03). The #5913 canary replays the SDK's real bwrap SETUP argv (`bwrap <canonical-argv> -- true`) under the committed seccomp profile. That replay **cannot** reproduce the #5849/#5873 **split-unshare EPERM**: bwrap 0.11.x combines all `--unshare-*` into one `unshare(…|NEWUSER)` (permitted by the #1557 allow-rule under both the committed and the pre-#5874 profiles), and the split — a *second* `unshare(NEWNS|NEWPID)` **without** NEWUSER — is a property of the claude CLI's nested-process structure, not of any bwrap-argv token. Empirically the real canonical argv passes **both** profiles.

The #5849 discrimination is covered at **merge** by `sandbox-canary-regression.test.sh` layer B (the argv-independent `unshare --user --map-root-user unshare --mount --pid` probe) run against the committed profile *file*. So a **profile** regression is caught pre-merge.

## The gap

A **kernel or bwrap-version regression on the prod host** that re-breaks *specifically the nested split* would **pass the deploy-time canary** (false-green for that one class) — because the deploy-time replay is argv-based and argv-replay can't reproduce the nested unshare, and layer B does not run in the prod container.

## The ask

Run the argv-independent nested-unshare probe (`unshare --user --map-root-user unshare --mount --pid`, the layer-B reproduction) **under the deployed profile inside the prod canary container** at deploy time, classify an EPERM as `sandbox_broken` (same verdict path as the existing `runReplay`), and surface it via the existing `feature:agent-sandbox` Sentry event. This closes the prod-side kernel/bwrap-version #5849 fidelity gap that the argv replay structurally cannot.

This is a **distinct capability** from "wire the real `--capture`" (#5913) — a new prod-container probe, not a fixture/argv concern. Out of #5913 scope by CTO ruling.

Refs #5913, #5889, #5875, ADR-079.

items.title: [Bubblewrap] platform_support() reports bubblewrap available where bwrap cannot create namespaces, and run() returns bwrap's failure as the workload's exit code

labels.name: Backend-Bubblewrap
labels.description: Linux process isolation implemented with Bubblewrap.

items.body:
## Relevant area(s)

Linux, Bubblewrap backend, host probing (`platform_support`, `available_backends`), `v1::run` / `v1::spawn`.

## Description

`v1::platform_support()` and `v1::available_backends()` decide that Bubblewrap is available by running `bwrap --version` and checking the version floor. That command never creates a namespace, so it succeeds on hosts where every real sandbox fails: inside a default Docker container (Docker's seccomp profile blocks `unshare`/`clone` with namespace flags), with `kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0`, or under Ubuntu 23.10+ AppArmor userns restrictions.

On such a host:

1. `platform_support()` returns `is_supported: true`, `available_methods: ["bubblewrap"]`, and no reason.
2. In the same answer (with slirp4netns and iptables installed, so the network walk reaches its namespace check), `bubblewrap_network.proxy_enforcement` is `Unsupported` with the warning "network.proxy requires unprivileged user and network namespaces, which this host refused (unshare --user --net exited with exit status: 1)". The network sub-probe already detects the problem; the backend probe does not.
3. `v1::run` returns `Ok` with `WaitResult::Exited(1)` and bwrap's diagnostic on the workload's stderr, instead of an `Error`. The caller cannot tell a sandbox that never started from a workload that exited 1, and `remediation` is never populated.

## Steps to reproduce

`Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "mxc-repro"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
mxc-sdk = "=1.0.0"
```

`src/main.rs`:

```rust
use mxc_sdk::v1::{self, ContainerRequest};

fn main() {
    let support = v1::platform_support();
    println!(
        "platform_support: supported={} methods={:?} reason={:?}",
        support.is_supported, support.available_methods, support.reason
    );
    println!("bubblewrap_network: {:?}", support.bubblewrap_network);
    match v1::run(ContainerRequest::new("echo hi"), Default::default()) {
        Ok(out) => {
            println!("outcome: {:?}", out.outcome);
            println!("stdout: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout));
            println!("stderr: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr));
        }
        Err(e) => println!(
            "error: code={:?} message={} remediation={:?}",
            e.code, e.message, e.remediation
        ),
    }
}
```

`Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile

WORKDIR /src
COPY Cargo.toml .
COPY src src
RUN cargo build --release

FROM debian:trixie-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends bubblewrap slirp4netns iptables && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN useradd -m app
USER app
CMD ["mxc-repro"]
```

```sh
docker build -t mxc-probe-repro .
docker run --rm mxc-probe-repro
```

Output (default Docker seccomp profile, no extra flags):

```
platform_support: supported=true methods=["bubblewrap"] reason=None
bubblewrap_network: Some(BubblewrapNetworkSupport { proxy_enforcement: Unsupported, warnings: ["Bubblewrap: network.proxy requires unprivileged user and network namespaces, which this host refused (unshare --user --net exited with exit status: 1). On Ubuntu 24.04+ this is usually AppArmor's 'kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1': give the caller an AppArmor profile that permits userns, or clear that sysctl on an ephemeral host. Otherwise enable the namespaces (for example 'sysctl -w kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1', or raise 'user.max_user_namespaces' / 'user.max_net_namespaces') or omit network.proxy."] })
outcome: Exited(1)
stdout: 
stderr: bwrap: No permissions to create a new namespace, likely because the kernel does not allow non-privileged user namespaces. See <https://deb.li/bubblewrap> or <file:///usr/share/doc/bubblewrap/README.Debian.gz>.
```

## Versions

- mxc-sdk 1.0.0 (crates.io); the same probe is on `main` at 2366ee9b1e0bed3a0f950ec49a509f92285239cf (2026-10-13)
- bubblewrap 0.12.0 (Debian 13 trixie package) inside the container
- Docker 29.7.2, default seccomp profile (`docker info`: `name=seccomp,profile=builtin`), cgroup v2
- Host: Linux 7.2.5 x86_64, unprivileged user namespaces enabled on the host

## Expected

- `platform_support()` reports `is_supported: false` (when no other backend is available), leaves `bubblewrap` out of `available_methods`, and gives bwrap's diagnostic as `reason`. `available_backends()` leaves Bubblewrap out or attaches the reason.
- `v1::run` / `v1::spawn` fail with `ErrorCode::BackendUnavailable` and a `remediation`, rather than reporting the workload as exited with code 1.

## Actual

`is_supported: true`, `available_methods: ["bubblewrap"]`, and `run` returns `Exited(1)` with `bwrap: No permissions to create a new namespace...` on stderr.

## Source

- `src/backends/bubblewrap/common/bwrap_version.rs:297-312`: `run_bwrap_version_until` runs `bwrap --version` only; `probe_bwrap` (line 227) caches that result.
- `src/core/mxc_engine/platform.rs:72-106`: `linux_platform_support_with` marks the host supported and adds `bubblewrap` when that version probe is `Ok`, then runs the proxy-enforcement probe, which does try `unshare --user --map-current-user --keep-caps --net` (`proxy_network.rs:1205`), but only uses its result for `bubblewrap_network`.
- `src/core/mxc_engine/probe.rs:140`: `linux_backends` uses the same `probe_bwrap()`.
- `src/backends/bubblewrap/common/bwrap_runner.rs:183`: pre-spawn validation calls `probe_bwrap_uncached` (version only), so nothing between the probe and the spawn notices.

## Suggested fix

After the version gate, run a trivial sandbox with the namespace set a real run uses (for example `bwrap --unshare-user --unshare-pid --unshare-ipc --unshare-uts --unshare-net --ro-bind-try /usr /usr ... --proc /proc --dev /dev -- true`), cache the result like the version, and report bwrap's stderr as `reason`. Two common failures deserve their own remediation text: `No permissions to create a new namespace` (seccomp, sysctl or AppArmor) and `Can't mount proc on /newroot/proc: Operation not permitted` (a container that masks `/proc` paths, fixed in Docker by `--security-opt systempaths=unconfined`). In `run`/`spawn`, a bwrap that exits before exec could be detected with a status pipe (`bwrap --info-fd` / `--json-status-fd` report the child pid once the sandbox is set up) and turned into `BackendUnavailable`.

## Related

Closed PR #752 ("fix(engine): probe real containment in platform_support()") proposed exactly this namespace probe and was closed without merging on 2026-09-25. I found no open issue tracking the problem: #769 is about a CI gate for probe coverage of new tiers and backends, #785 is a Windows `captureDenials` probe mismatch, and #994 / #1029 added the network support tier. Searches for "No permissions to create a new namespace", "docker", "user namespace" and "probe bubblewrap" found nothing else.

items.title: Never signal process group 0 or 1: a test's fake pid logged out the desktop
items.body:
## What happened

Running the test suite on a desktop logged the whole session out (GNOME, twice). The journal shows `ssh-agent`, `gnome-keyring-daemon`, Xwayland and D-Bus all receiving SIGTERM at the same instant.

`tests/test_bg_tool_gates.py::test_bg_release_kills_and_snaps_output` gives `_acp_terminal_release` a fake process with `pid = 1`. The release path goes:

```
_acp_terminal_release → _terminal_close → _kill_terminal_proc
  → os.killpg(1, SIGTERM)
  → os.killpg(1, SIGKILL)   # terminal.py escalation
```

glibc implements `killpg(g)` as `kill(-g)`, so **pgid 1 is `kill(-1)`: every process the user owns gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL**. pgid 0 would be our own process group, which includes the editor.

## Fix

- `bridge/acp/terminal.py`: add `_safe_killpg()`, used at all three `killpg` sites. It refuses pid ≤ 1 and non-int pids (bools included) and raises `ProcessLookupError`, so callers fall back to `proc.terminate()` / `proc.kill()`. Terminal children are spawned with `start_new_session=True`, so a real pgid is always > 1 and no legitimate kill is blocked.
- `tests/test_bg_tool_gates.py`: the `pid = 1` test now mocks `os.killpg` and asserts it is never reached.
- `tests/conftest.py`: suite-wide guard. Under pytest, `os.kill` / `os.killpg` on pid ≤ 1 raise `AssertionError` instead of signalling the desktop.
- `tests/test_safe_killpg.py`: pins the guard and the `terminate()` fallback.

## Testing

Full suite run inside a PID namespace (`unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --mount-proc`), where even `kill(-1)` only reaches the sandbox: 1301 passed, 6 skipped, 1 failed. The failure is `test_context_images::test_a_queued_prompt_keeps_its_context_for_the_send`, which fails the same way on unmodified `master`.

Until this lands, anyone running the suite outside a sandbox gets logged out.

### What's wrong

With `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1`, every Bash tool call fails before the command runs:

```
bwrap: Can't mkdir /root/actions-runner-2/.claude: Permission denied
```

This looks like a variant of #79997 (fixed in 2.1.227) that still occurs on 2.1.281.

### Environment

- Claude Code 2.1.281 (native), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, bubblewrap 0.9.0, `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`.
- Claude runs as **root**. The cwd is `/root/actions-runner-2/_work/<repo>/<repo>` (a second self-hosted GitHub Actions runner).
- `/root/actions-runner-2` is owned by **uid 1001** with mode 755, as extracted from GitHub's runner tarball. All directories below it are owned by root.

### Cause (from the captured bwrap argv)

The sandbox adds denyWrite entries for `<ancestor>/.claude` (and `.mcp.json`) at every ancestor of the cwd, and for missing paths it adds `--ro-bind /tmp/claude-empty-XXXX <ancestor>/.claude`. bwrap runs with `--unshare-user --cap-drop ALL`. Inside that user namespace, uid 1001 is unmapped, so root has no DAC override on `/root/actions-runner-2` and cannot create the mount-point stub. The stubs under root-owned ancestors (`_work/.claude`, `_work/<repo>/.claude`) are fine.

A minimal bwrap test on the same host shows the same result:

```
bwrap --unshare-pid --unshare-user --cap-drop ALL --ro-bind / / --bind /tmp /tmp \
  --ro-bind /tmp/empty /tmp/t/u1001/.claude true   # fails: Can't mkdir ... Permission denied
# same command with /tmp/t/u0 (owned by root) succeeds
```

### Expected

A missing ancestor stub that cannot be created should not kill every Bash call. For example, the fix from #79997 could also cover ancestors that the process owner cannot write to inside the user namespace, not only root-owned ancestors seen by a non-root user.
