items.title: Secure mode never gives apply-seccomp CAP_SYS_ADMIN: --cap-drop ALL empties the bounding set, so the nested-userns fallback cannot work
items.body:
<!--
Paste-ready issue for anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime (no issue template in that repo, so this is free-form). Lines are intentionally unwrapped for GitHub. All source references pinned to e5fb1b9 = current main = v0.0.74.

Suggested title: Secure mode never gives apply-seccomp CAP_SYS_ADMIN: --cap-drop ALL empties the bounding set, so the nested-userns fallback cannot work
-->

## Summary

In secure mode the bwrap invocation passes `--cap-drop ALL`, which empties the capability **bounding set**. That makes both of `apply-seccomp`'s routes to `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` unavailable at once:

- **path (a)** — "the caller (bwrap) kept `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in this user namespace via `--cap-add`" — is never enabled, because no `--cap-add` is ever passed;
- **path (b)** — create a nested user namespace to obtain the capability — cannot grant any capability either, because a user namespace cannot grant what the bounding set no longer contains.

So `apply-seccomp` falls into path (b) and dies writing the new namespace's map:

```
apply-seccomp: write /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted
```

This is the failure mode the code already anticipates at [`apply-seccomp.c:694-699`](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L694-L699) — "the unshare succeeds but the new namespace grants no capabilities … the caller must supply CAP_SYS_ADMIN" — but attributed there to an LSM gate. Here there is no LSM gate; the caller's own `--cap-drop ALL` produces it.

It surfaces when the runtime is already inside an unprivileged user namespace (rootless container, `bwrap --unshare-user` wrapper), where path (b)'s map write has no privileged fallback. Downstream report, where this removes the Bash tool entirely: anthropics/claude-code#89478. Claude Code 2.1.212 works; 2.1.220 through 2.1.236 fail.

## The two paths, and why both are closed

All references pinned to [`e5fb1b9`](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/commit/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf) (current `main`, v0.0.74).

[`vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c:685-699`](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L685-L699):

```c
    /* ---- New PID + mount namespaces. Children (not us) enter the PID ns. ----
     *
     * Two paths to get CAP_SYS_ADMIN for the unshare:
     *   (a) The caller (bwrap) kept CAP_SYS_ADMIN in this user namespace via
     *       --cap-add. Just unshare directly.
     *   (b) We don't have the cap. Create a nested user namespace to get it,
     *       map uid/gid, then unshare. ...
```

[`src/sandbox/linux-sandbox-utils.ts:1946-1966`](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/src/sandbox/linux-sandbox-utils.ts#L1946-L1966):

```ts
    if (!enableWeakerNestedSandbox) {
      // ...
      // apply-seccomp does not need caps here — it creates its own nested
      // userns to obtain CAP_SYS_ADMIN for its PID+mount unshare (see below).
      bwrapArgs.push('--unshare-user', '--cap-drop', 'ALL', '--proc', '/proc')
    } else {
      // ...
      bwrapArgs.push('--unshare-user', '--bind', '/proc', '/proc')
    }
```

`--cap-add` appears nowhere in the TypeScript — it occurs only in those two apply-seccomp comments ([688-689](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L688-L689), [834-836](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L834-L836)). Path (a) is therefore dead code as shipped, and the comment at 1953-1954 ("apply-seccomp does not need caps here") holds only where path (b) can still bootstrap a capability-bearing user namespace.

The measured consequence, inside an unprivileged user namespace on an unrestricted host:

```
--cap-drop ALL      ->  CapBnd: 0000000000000000   CapEff: 0000000000000000
                        and inside a freshly created nested userns:  CapEff: 0000000000000000
```

With an empty bounding set the nested namespace confers nothing, so the `/proc/self/{setgroups,uid_map,gid_map}` writes at [737-746](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L737-L746) fail and the process dies at [743](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L743).

## Reproduction

Host: Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS, kernel `7.0.11-76070011-generic` x86_64, bubblewrap 0.11.0. Unprivileged user namespaces unrestricted (`user.max_user_namespaces=2147483647`, no `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns`), so the LSM caveat in the README does not apply.

Run all of this **inside** an unprivileged user namespace, e.g. under `bwrap --unshare-user …`, to model a rootless container:

```sh
BW="bwrap --ro-bind /usr /usr --ro-bind /etc /etc --symlink usr/bin /bin --symlink usr/lib /lib --symlink usr/lib64 /lib64 --dev /dev --unshare-pid --unshare-user"

# 1. Secure mode as shipped (line 1955). Bounding set empty; nested userns grants nothing.
$BW --proc /proc --cap-drop ALL -- sh -c '
  grep -E "CapBnd|CapEff" /proc/self/status
  unshare -U sh -c "grep CapEff /proc/self/status"   # caps inside the path-(b) namespace
  unshare --pid --mount --fork true'                 # path (a)
#   CapBnd: 0000000000000000
#   CapEff: 0000000000000000
#   CapEff: 0000000000000000        <- nested userns confers no capability
#   unshare: unshare() failed: Operation not permitted

# 2. Weaker mode (line 1965). Caps retained, path (a) succeeds outright.
$BW --bind /proc /proc -- sh -c 'grep CapBnd /proc/self/status; unshare --pid --mount --fork true && echo "path (a): OK"'
#   CapBnd: 000001ffffffffff
#   path (a): OK

# 3. Proposed fix. Everything dropped except the one capability apply-seccomp asks for.
$BW --proc /proc --cap-drop ALL --cap-add CAP_SYS_ADMIN -- sh -c 'grep CapEff /proc/self/status; unshare --pid --mount --fork true && echo "path (a): OK"'
#   CapEff: 0000000000200000        <- CAP_SYS_ADMIN only
#   path (a): OK
```

A note for anyone reproducing the *exact* die message with a shell rather than the real binary: a plain shell fails one step earlier, on the `setgroups` write at [737](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L737) with `EACCES`, because it lacks the `PR_SET_DUMPABLE` flip that `apply-seccomp` performs at [731-732](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L731-L732). The real binary clears that hurdle and then dies on the `uid_map` write at 743, which is the message users report.

## Version evidence

String search over the shipped Claude Code executables, which bundle this runtime:

| Claude Code | `--cap-drop` | `--cap-add` | Bash inside a nested userns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1.212 | absent | absent | works |
| 2.1.231 | present | absent | fails |
| 2.1.236 | present | absent | fails |

The regression tracks the introduction of `--cap-drop ALL`, and no build has ever paired it with `--cap-add`.

## Suggested fix

Pass the capability apply-seccomp documents that it needs, at [line 1955](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/src/sandbox/linux-sandbox-utils.ts#L1955):

```ts
bwrapArgs.push('--unshare-user', '--cap-drop', 'ALL', '--cap-add', 'CAP_SYS_ADMIN', '--proc', '/proc')
```

This restores path (a), so the nested-userns bootstrap is never attempted and the environment-dependent map write disappears from the common path. It also makes the runtime match its own documentation.

The workload's confinement is unchanged. `apply-seccomp` clears the ambient set at [837](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L837) once the mount is done, sets `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` at [859](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L859), and `execvp`s the command at [871](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L871) — exactly the sequence the comment at 834-836 describes — so the command begins with an empty effective set plus the seccomp filter.

Two things worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting:

- **Bounding set.** `--cap-add CAP_SYS_ADMIN` leaves `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the worker's bounding set. `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` plus the absence of file capabilities on anything reachable means the workload cannot regain it, so this is defensible; adding `PR_CAPBSET_DROP` for the worker after the mount would close it outright and cost nothing.
- **The remount concern the current code is guarding.** The comment at [1948-1953](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/src/sandbox/linux-sandbox-utils.ts#L1948-L1953) motivates `--cap-drop ALL` by the risk of a root parent leaving the sandboxed command able to remount `rw` over `--ro-bind / /`. Granting one capability to `apply-seccomp`, which strips it before exec, does not reopen that: the shell/command past `execvp` still has nothing. The current arrangement pays for that guarantee by removing the capability apply-seccomp itself needs.

If granting the capability is unacceptable, the fallback options are strictly worse but still better than today:

1. Detect the empty bounding set (or a failed path (b)) and emit the actionable message the `setgroups` branch already carries at [738-740](https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime/blob/e5fb1b93ba61bab8e916bee7541860bbdaa612cf/vendor/seccomp-src/apply-seccomp.c#L738-L740) — "nested userns is capability-restricted; caller must provide CAP_SYS_ADMIN" — for the `uid_map`/`gid_map` writes at 743 and 746 too, instead of a bare `EPERM`. Right now the one branch that explains the problem is the one branch users do not hit.
2. Have the caller detect this case and fall back to the `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` argument shape automatically, rather than requiring users to discover an undocumented setting after their sandbox stops working.

## Cross-reference

Downstream: anthropics/claude-code#89478 (Bash tool refused since 2.1.220; 2.1.212 works). Filed here because the mechanism and the fix both live in this repo.

items.title: Sessions run in their own PID namespace so an agent cannot see or signal host processes outside its tree
items.body:
## Problem
A session's backend runs as the operator's OS user. Every process under that user is visible to the agent's `ps`/`pgrep` and can be signalled by it: other sessions, long-running host services, the operator's own dev servers. An agent that matches a command line by pattern and assumes the match is its own leftover can kill a same-user service, and nothing below the agent stops it. Prompt rules cannot close this, because `pgrep` and `kill` are legitimate tools. Only the process boundary can.

## Approach
1. On Linux, launch each session backend in its own PID namespace, keeping the current uid mapping (unprivileged user namespace, e.g. `unshare --user --map-current-user --pid --fork --mount-proc` or bubblewrap). Network and filesystem stay shared.
2. Probe support once at service start, since user namespaces can be disabled by sysctl or LSM policy. When unsupported, launch as today and report `pid_isolation: unavailable` in `baton status`.
3. Inventory in-session helpers that probe or signal pids outside the session tree (liveness `kill -0`, reapers) and route them through the service API or host-side execution.
4. macOS and Windows report `unavailable`. Out of scope here.

## Acceptance criteria
- On a Linux host with user namespaces, a session's `ps -e` lists only its own tree, and `kill <pid>` against a host process of the same user fails.
- Inside an isolated session, git, gh, network access, file edits and killing the agent's own child processes behave as before.
- Existing liveness and reap tests pass with isolation on.
- With user namespaces unavailable, sessions launch unchanged and `baton status` reports isolation unavailable.

items.title: hermes desktop forces --no-sandbox even when an AppArmor userns profile makes the Electron sandbox work

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

items.body:
## Summary

`hermes desktop` forces `--no-sandbox` on hosts where **the Electron sandbox already works**, because
the decision is made from the sysctl alone and the accompanying probe cannot observe an AppArmor
`userns` profile that grants namespaces to the packaged binary.

Symptom on Ubuntu 24.04+ / 26.04 (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 1`):

```
→ Configuring Electron Linux sandbox helper (sudo required)...
✗ Failed to configure Electron's Linux sandbox helper: …/apps/desktop/release/linux-unpacked/chrome-sandbox
⚠ Falling back to --no-sandbox because this Linux host restricts unprivileged user namespaces …
```

The 4755 helper route needs root, so on a machine without passwordless sudo the fallback is the only
outcome the code can reach — even though Ubuntu's own documented workaround (a per-executable AppArmor
profile granting `userns`, shipped by Ubuntu for other Electron apps, e.g. `/etc/apparmor.d/anythingllmdesktop`)
makes the namespace sandbox work.

## Mechanism

- `_desktop_linux_needs_no_sandbox()` (`hermes_cli/main_desktop.py:1090` @ `34e09bff`) returns `True`
  purely from `/proc/sys/kernel/apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns == "1"`.
- Its companion `_desktop_linux_userns_sandbox_available()` (line 1108) probes with
  `unshare --user --map-root-user true` **from the CLI process, which is unconfined** — the restriction
  applies to it, so it fails with `write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted`.

The profile confines the *Electron* program, not the *probing CLI*, so the probe can never observe the
user's hardening. Result: the hardening is applied, verified working, and then ignored at launch.

## Evidence

With this profile installed:

```
# /etc/apparmor.d/hermes-desktop
profile hermes-desktop /**/apps/desktop/release/linux-unpacked/Hermes flags=(unconfined) { userns, }
```

- packaged binary launched **without any flag** → survives startup, no `setuid_sandbox_host` abort,
  renderer sandbox functional;
- `hermes desktop` still appends `--no-sandbox`, so the launched app runs sandbox-less.

(The same experiment on a Fabric AppImage with its own `userns` profile: sandbox works, and removing
`--no-sandbox` from the launcher was verified end-to-end.)

## Suggested fixes

- Consult the profile rather than the sysctl alone: probe through it
  (`aa-exec -p <profile> -- unshare --user --map-root-user true`), or treat a loaded `userns` profile
  whose attachment pattern matches the packaged executable as "userns available" before falling back.
- At minimum, the fallback message should name the AppArmor profile as an alternative to the sudo/4755
  route — users without passwordless sudo cannot take the route the message implies, and the current
  wording suggests the only fix requires root.

## Related work (checked before filing)

- **#86718** (open) probes "can *this process* create a user namespace" — but it probes from the
  unconfined CLI process, so on a host like this one it fails exactly the same way and still falls
  back to `--no-sandbox`. Same blind spot as today's `_desktop_linux_userns_sandbox_available()`.
- **#100999** (open) escalates the 4755-helper route via `sudo -n`/`pkexec` — helps hosts with
  passwordless sudo/polkit, not hosts without either (and a root-owned 4755 helper isn't the only
  rootless option; the AppArmor profile route needs root only once, to install the profile).
- **#95235**, **#97404**, **#96687** (open) and **#51327**/**#96442** (closed) cover the
  chrome-sandbox/setuid fallback family; none of them consult a loaded AppArmor `userns` profile.

## Environment

- Ubuntu 24.04+/26.04 (unprivileged user namespaces restricted), no passwordless sudo, no polkit
  escalation
- git install, main @ `34e09bff`; packaged app at `apps/desktop/release/linux-unpacked/`

items.title: fix(desktop): keep chrome-sandbox setuid in Linux packages
items.body:
### Issue for this PR

Closes #58157

### Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Refactor / code improvement
- [ ] Documentation

### What does this PR do?

The deb installs `/opt/OpenCode/chrome-sandbox` as 0755, so on AppArmor-confined systems (Ubuntu 24+) Chromium falls back to user namespaces, the main process gains NoNewPrivs, every child inherits it, pkexec can never elevate, and in-app updates die with `pkexec must be setuid root` (exit 127).

The mode does not come from staged files: electron-builder's default postinst probes `unshare --user true` in dpkg's unconfined context and deliberately resets 0755 on every install/update. So this replaces the postinst for deb/rpm (all channels) with `scripts/after-install.sh` — the default template with the sandbox block forced to unconditional `chmod 4755`, matching what other Electron debs ship. A root-owned 4755 helper is safe with and without working user namespaces.

### How did you verify your code works?

- Contract table in `electron-builder.config.test.ts`: every channel's deb/rpm resolves to the script and the script carries the unconditional setuid line. Full file 10 pass, 100/100 over `--rerun-each 10`; `bun typecheck` clean in `packages/desktop`.
- Rendered the script with prod vars and ran it twice against a staged 0755 helper: 755 -> 4755 on install, stays 4755 on update (other errors in the log are sandbox artifacts: no /usr/bin write, no real executable — the script continues past them as designed).
- `bash -n` clean on source and rendered script.

### Screenshots / recordings

Not a UI change. Functional proof from the rendered-script run:

```
$ stat -c '%a' sbtest/opt/TestApp/chrome-sandbox
755
$ bash sbtest/rendered.sh   # install
$ stat -c '%a' sbtest/opt/TestApp/chrome-sandbox
4755
$ bash sbtest/rendered.sh   # update

4755
```

items.title: exec: default RLIMIT_NPROC=64 makes unprivileged mediated execution unusable on hosts where the invoking user owns >=64 processes (fork EAGAIN)
items.body:
## Summary

`arbitraitor-exec`'s default `ResourceLimits::process_count = Some(64)` makes unprivileged mediated script execution unusable on any host where the invoking user owns ≥64 processes. The limit is applied as `RLIMIT_NPROC` via the fenced prlimit sequence (`SIGSTOP` → `prlimit` → `SIGCONT`) in `ScriptExecution::execute` (`crates/arbitraitor-exec/src/spawn.rs`), but Linux checks `RLIMIT_NPROC` against the **real UID's system-wide** process count. Inside the `unshare --user --map-current-user --net` wrapper the real UID is unchanged, so the limit is evaluated against the *host* user's full process table — not the sandboxed child.

## Mechanism

- `ResourceLimits::default()` sets `process_count: Some(64)` (`crates/arbitraitor-exec/src/lib.rs`).
- `apply_limits_fenced` applies it as `RLIMIT_NPROC` to the stopped child before `SIGCONT` (`crates/arbitraitor-exec/src/spawn.rs`).
- The mediated Linux path wraps the interpreter in `unshare --user --map-current-user --net --` (`build_program_command`). `--map-current-user` maps the caller's own UID to itself; the **real UID is unchanged**, so `fork()` inside the wrapper hits `EAGAIN` whenever uid's process count ≥ 64+ (kernel compares against the user's process count, allowing a small headroom via `threads-max` heuristics).

## Live evidence (this workstation, zero Orchestraitor code involved)

Host: Linux 7.2.9, ~1038 processes owned by the invoking uid (1000).

Vendor-controlled repro — no Orchestraitor code, only the pinned `arbitraitor-exec` default plus bash:

```console
$ ulimit -u 64; /bin/bash --noprofile --norc -c "env -0 | wc -c"
/bin/bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
/bin/bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
/bin/bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
/bin/bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
/bin/bash: fork: Resource temporarily unavailable
rc=254
```

Same-shaped contrast at the same `ulimit -u 64`:

- single builtins succeed (`printf`, `true`, `echo`, non-forking redirections like `true > file`) — no `fork()` needed;
- **any** external command or pipeline member fails identically (`/usr/bin/env -0`, `/bin/echo hi > file`, `env -0 | wc -c`) — each requires one `fork()`.

Downstream observation (orchestraitor, `mediated_bash_env` test): same worker returns `exit_code = Some(254)`, stderr = 5× `fork: retry`, stdout = empty; the next script in the same worker (`printf 'p=%s h=%s' "$PATH" "$HOME"`) returns exit 0 with `p=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin h=/tmp/arbitraitor-exec-<pid>-<n>` — proving the controlled PATH and temp HOME are correctly constructed and the *only* failure mode is the fork limit.

## Impact

- **Host-dependent failures:** mediated exec passes on quiet CI runners (invoking user < 64 processes) and fails on desktops / busy shared runners. The same binary is deterministic on a given host but not portable across hosts — a correctness and test-reliability defect, not a flake.
- **Downstream block:** orchestraitor issue [#494](https://github.com/arbsec/orchestraitor/issues/494) (`mediated_bash_env_is_allowlisted_and_path_is_controlled`) fails with the misleading assertion "controlled PATH missing in child" — the child never ran; its `env -0` forked and died. That test's skip-gate runs `run_bash(b"true\n")`, which passes precisely because `true` is a builtin and needs no fork, so the gate cannot detect a fork-hostile host.

## Fix directions (either, or both)

1. **Fail closed with a typed error:** at context build or fenced-apply time, compute/validate `process_count` against the invoking user's actual system-wide process count (as the kernel will under the unprivileged user namespace) and return a typed `ExecError::ResourceLimit` instead of letting bash die with exit 254 and empty stdout.
2. **Preflight probe datum:** expose an NPROC-viability probe (analogous to the existing `unshare` capability probe in `network_namespace_supported`-style gates) so callers (e.g. orchestraitor's `mediated_stack_or_skip`) can skip or fail cleanly with an accurate reason instead of misattributing the failure.

A caller-side override of `process_count` is *not* an acceptable fix for consumers: it would unilaterally loosen a containment default outside Arbitraitor's enforcement boundary.

Refs: arbsec/orchestraitor#494; spec.md §185 ("Defaults should ... enforce reasonable resource limits").

items.title: Allow Bazel kernel sandboxing on the AppArmor-restricted runner
items.body:
## Problem and change

The P330 runner cannot start the Bazel kernel build used by the full VS image workflow. In [PR #30's failed run](https://github.com/securely1g/sonic-buildimage/actions/runs/40255619811), `@sonic_linux_kernel//:kernel_packages` requests `SonicKernelBuild=linux-sandbox`, but Bazel reports that this strategy is unavailable before executing any kernel actions.

The runner uses Ubuntu 26.04. Its AppArmor policy moves the non-root sandbox process into `unprivileged_userns`, which denies the mount operation needed to isolate the build. Privileged Docker alone does not resolve that host policy denial.

Install an AppArmor profile for the kernel workspace's `linux-sandbox` executable, and check its configuration during runner preflight. Bootstrap and manager installation include the helper. The installer parses the policy before loading it, loads only this profile, and refuses to replace conflicting administrator policy or symlinks.

## Concrete before/after

These results come from the same P330 host, `sonic-slave-trixie:4b8b34e9bb1`, Bazel 8.5.1 and build user UID 1001. The historical build directory had been removed, so the reproduction uses a fresh kernel-shaped directory. [Before/after run and logs](https://github.com/securely1g/sonic-buildimage/actions/runs/40263017467).

| Input or action | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run the installed kernel-workspace `linux-sandbox -- /bin/true` with an empty environment | Exit 1: `mount: Permission denied`; audit log: `profile="unprivileged_userns" operation="mount" name="/"` | Exit 0 with the scoped profile loaded |
| Read `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` | `1` | `1` |
| Run unrelated `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount /bin/true` | Exit 1 | Exit 1 |

The attachment is limited to `/sonic/target/bazel-kernel-state/*/build/output/install/*/linux-sandbox`. items.title: [Bug]: Linux shared-folder lookup in a user namespace corrupts cached ownership and denies access outside the namespace
items.body:
### Version

7.2.14

### Host OS Type

Linux

### Host OS name + version

Pop!_OS 22.04 LTS

### Host Architecture

x86

### Guest OS Type

Linux

### Guest Architecture

x86

### Guest OS name + version

Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS

### Component

Guest Additions/Shared Folders

### What happened?

Previously accessible directories in a read-only VirtualBox share became selectively inaccessible from the Linux guest. The share, named `host`, exposes the host user's home directory and is automounted at `/media/sf_host`. My user first noticed the problem while working with Codex to locate and copy documents from the host's pCloud and Dropbox directories. They did not recall changing the share configuration or permissions before the failure.

The symptoms were confusing: `ls /media/sf_host/pcloud` could list the expected top-level contents, but a recursive `find` failed with Permission denied. My user ran the same `find` in a separate ordinary guest terminal and confirmed that it also failed. Their `tree` reported `[error opening dir]` for several, but not all, pCloud subdirectories. I then ran a broader `tree /media/sf_host/`, which showed many other ordinary host directories were inaccessible while parts of pCloud remained readable.

My user also observed the problem in the guest's Files application, where affected directories displayed lock icons. Opening `desktop` (a symlink to `Desktop`) produced: "You do not have the permissions necessary to view the contents of \"desktop\"." This was therefore not confined to Codex or its sandbox.

My initial inspection showed a discrepancy between the mount's configured ownership (`uid=0,gid=981,dmode=0770,fmode=0770`) and guest-visible metadata reporting `65534:65534` (`nobody:nogroup`) with mode `0770`. The guest account was a member of `vboxsf`. These observations did not initially explain why some paths remained readable and others did not; changing group membership was not an adequate explanation or remedy.

At my user's request, I compared the guest configuration with the expected setup and found no configuration error explaining the failure. I subsequently traced the suspected cause to the driver's inode ownership initialization and developed a standalone `unshare` reproduction. My user helped simplify it into the two-order command below and ran it to confirm the result.

Expected: the authorized guest user should retain access to the shared directories. A read-only inspection by another process, including one in a user namespace, should not change ownership or access for ordinary guest processes. The controlled reproduction below isolates that access-order dependency without requiring Codex or any other application sandbox.

#### Suspected cause

The installed Guest Additions source, `src/vboxguest-7.2.14/vboxsf/utils.c`, contains the following in `vbsf_init_inode()`:

```c
inode->i_uid = make_kuid(current_user_ns(), pSuperInfo->uid);
inode->i_gid = make_kgid(current_user_ns(), pSuperInfo->gid);
```

These assignments are also present in the [public main-branch source](https://github.com/VirtualBox/virtualbox/blob/main/src/VBox/Additions/linux/sharedfolders/utils.c).

In the standalone reproducer, the requesting namespace maps only internal UID/GID 1000 to the launching root identity. The mount's configured UID 0 and GID 981 have no mapping there. Interpreting the mount options in the lookup process's namespace appears to produce invalid IDs which are then stored in the shared inode. This is an explanation inferred from source inspection and the experiments, rather than a tested patch.

#### Related reports and scope

[Flathub qBittorrent issue #62](https://github.com/flathub/org.qbittorrent.qBittorrent/issues/62), opened in 2021, describes very similar ownership changes, recovery after remounting, and successful sandboxed access when the ordinary application accesses the directory first. An August 2026 comment reports continued failures. Whether it has precisely the same cause has not been independently verified.

We have reproduced this on 7.2.14. We have not tested newer releases or development builds; finding the same assignments in main is not a runtime test of those versions.

### How can we reproduce this?

Run the following block in an ordinary non-root guest Bash terminal. It tests both lookup orders, unmounting between them to reset the inode cache, and removes its mount directory afterward. This exact block was tested on the configuration above on 2026-10-07.

**DO NOT RUN AS ROOT**

Run the block from your ordinary guest user's shell, not a root shell or under an outer `sudo`. The unprefixed `stat` and `ls` must test that user's access, not root's privileges. Keep the individual `sudo` commands inside the block as written.

The second `ls` is expected to fail; any other error invalidates the comparison and may require manual unmounting before retrying.

```bash
(
    repro_mount=/mnt/vbox-userns-test
    repro_share=host
    repro_folder=vbox_test
    repro_gid=981
    sudo mkdir "$repro_mount"
    sudo mount -t vboxsf -o "ro,nodev,nosuid,uid=0,gid=$repro_gid,dmode=0770,fmode=0770" "$repro_share" "$repro_mount"
    stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$repro_mount/$repro_folder"
    sudo unshare --user --map-user=1000 --map-group=1000 -- stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$repro_mount/$repro_folder"
    ls "$repro_mount/$repro_folder" # Expected: succeeds.
    sudo umount "$repro_mount"
    sudo mount -t vboxsf -o "ro,nodev,nosuid,uid=0,gid=$repro_gid,dmode=0770,fmode=0770" "$repro_share" "$repro_mount"
    sudo unshare --user --map-user=1000 --map-group=1000 -- stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$repro_mount/$repro_folder"
    stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$repro_mount/$repro_folder"
    ls "$repro_mount/$repro_folder" # Expected on affected driver: Permission denied.
    sudo umount "$repro_mount"
    sudo rmdir "$repro_mount"
)
```

[VBox.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33157281/VBox.log)

Output from my user's test run, omitting the sudo password prompt:

```text
0:981 770 /mnt/vbox-userns-test/vbox_test
1000:65534 770 /mnt/vbox-userns-test/vbox_test
VBox.log
65534:65534 770 /mnt/vbox-userns-test/vbox_test
65534:65534 770 /mnt/vbox-userns-test/vbox_test
ls: cannot open directory '/mnt/vbox-userns-test/vbox_test': Permission denied
```

In the ordinary-first phase, ownership is correctly initialized as `0:981`. The namespace's `1000:65534` is the expected translation of that ownership into its own ID mapping, and the ordinary listing succeeds (`VBox.log` is the test directory's sole entry).

After remounting, the namespace-first lookup produces `65534:65534`. Crucially, the following ordinary lookup now also reports `65534:65534`, and the ordinary listing fails. The same directory and mount options therefore give different access results solely from reversing lookup order.

On this Ubuntu installation, unprivileged `unshare --user --map-current-user` was denied while writing `uid_map`, so the reproducer uses `sudo` to establish the namespace without changing system-wide namespace restrictions.

### Did you upload *all* of your necessary log files, screenshots, etc.?

- [x] Yes, I've uploaded all pertinent files to this issue.

items.title: linux: don't truncate cgroup v2 cpu.max
items.body:
Fixes #5374

uv__get_cgroupv2_constrained_cpu() reads cpu.max into a 16 byte buffer,
so uv__slurp() keeps at most 15 characters. A cpu.max line of 16 or more
characters, e.g. "15840000 1000000" from the issue, loses the last digit
of the period: the quota is computed as 15840000 / 100000 = 158 instead
of 15, which is larger than the CPU count, so uv_available_parallelism()
ignores the cgroup limit. This affects any 1s period with a quota of 10
or more CPUs. #4746 changed the code to read cpu.max directly into the
16 byte quota_buf; before that the file was read into a 1024 byte buffer.

This change reads cpu.max into the function's existing 1024 byte buffer
again. Nothing else in the cgroup v2 or v1 code paths is changed.

Test: platform_cgroup2_cpu_max (in test/test-platform-output.c) unshares
user, mount and cgroup namespaces, mounts a tmpfs over /sys/fs/cgroup,
writes cpu.max and checks uv_available_parallelism() for
"9000000 1000000" (15 characters, 9) and "15840000 1000000" (16
characters, 15). The truncation only changes the result when the
process may run on at least 16 CPUs, so the test skips on smaller
machines. It also skips when unprivileged user namespaces or the tmpfs
mount are not allowed (e.g. AppArmor-restricted user namespaces on
Ubuntu 24.04) and on non-cgroup v2 systems, so it will likely be
skipped in CI.

Testing (Linux x86_64, gcc 14.2, 8 CPUs):
- With sched_getaffinity() shimmed to report 16 CPUs via LD_PRELOAD,
  the new test fails without the fix (15 == 16) and passes with it,
  for uv_run_tests and uv_run_tests_a.
- Full suite, cmake + Ninja + ctest -V, before and after: identical
  results apart from the new test. getaddrinfo_fail and
  getaddrinfo_fail_sync fail in both runs because of the local DNS
  resolver.
- -DASAN=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug: full uv_run_tests_a run, same
  results before and after, no sanitizer reports; the new test also
  passes under ASAN with the 16 CPU shim.
- autotools: ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make, plus building and
  running test/run-tests.

Not tested: 32-bit, non-Linux platforms, make distcheck.

envtest Stop() times out on hosts whose hostname exceeds 63 bytes (kube-apiserver identity lease label)
items.body:
**Summary:** on a host whose hostname is longer than 63 bytes, `testEnv.Stop()` fails with `timeout waiting for process kube-apiserver to stop`. The macOS GitHub runners have such hostnames, so `test.sh` fails in AfterSuite of `pkg/applyconfiguration/testdata/cronjob` on `macos-latest` while every spec passes.

**Cause:** kube-apiserver puts the hostname into a label value of its identity lease. A label value is limited to 63 bytes, so every lease update is rejected (`must be no more than 63 bytes`, every 7 s), and the apiserver's graceful shutdown never finishes.

**Reproduction (Linux, envtest assets v1.36.0):**

- `unshare --user --map-root-user --uts`, set the hostname, run `go test ./...` in `pkg/applyconfiguration/testdata/cronjob`.
- 63-byte hostname: passes in 4 s.
- 64-byte hostname: AfterSuite fails at `suite_test.go:65` with `timeout waiting for process kube-apiserver to stop` after 20 s; reproduced twice.

**Workaround:** shorten the runner hostname before the tests (`sudo scutil --set HostName <short>; sudo hostname <short>`). Results of the workaround on a fork CI run: https://github.com/lusoris/controller-tools/actions/runs/39590276867 (macOS job 119189216012: hostname shortened from 67 to 4 bytes, `test.sh` passed).

Happy to open a pull request with the workflow step if that is the preferred fix; the underlying limit is in kube-apiserver.

items.title: fix(build / ci): guard recovery compares start ticks across Linux time namespaces
items.body:
### Subsystem

build / ci (TypeScript, Rust, WASM, bundling)

### Priority

P3

### Defect

The Linux guard storage recovery excuse (PR 5355) compares a dead supervisor's recorded /proc start ticks with ticks the reclaimer reads for an uninspectable same-account process. /proc/<pid>/stat field 22 is reported relative to the reader's time namespace (fs/proc/array.c do_task_stat uses timens_add_boottime_ns with the reader's offsets), so ticks recorded by a supervisor inside a time namespace with a boottime offset are not comparable with ticks read by a reclaimer outside it. A non-dumpable descendant of such a supervisor could then read as started before it, be excused, and lose storage it still holds. Expected: record the supervisor's time-namespace identity (for example the /proc/self/ns/time inode) with its ticks and drop the excuse when the reclaimer's differs, or document the limit beside the existing one.

### Reproduce

1. On Linux, start a guarded command inside unshare --user --map-current-user --time --boottime +N, with a non-dumpable descendant that keeps its cwd in the run storage.
2. SIGKILL the guard; from the root time namespace start another guarded command, which recovers the abandoned storage.
3. The descendant reads as started before the recorded supervisor ticks and is excused, so the storage is removed while it is held (traced from code; not run).

### References

PR 5355, PR 5345, #5347

items.title: Linux confinement: under the unshare fallback the command is namespace root and can umount the tmpfs hiding the holdout store
items.body:
## What happens
On Linux without `bwrap`, `confine::prefix` falls back to `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount -- /bin/sh -c UNSHARE_SCRIPT …`, which mounts an empty tmpfs over each hidden root and then `exec`s the command. The command runs as uid 0 of a user namespace that owns the new mount namespace, with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` there, and the tmpfs mounts were made inside that namespace, so they are not locked: the confined command can simply `umount <root>` and read the real holdout store underneath.

```sh
umount ~/.kyvor/work 2>/dev/null; cat ~/.kyvor/work/<org>/<project>/holdout/<case>
# (spelled so the bash mention heuristic does not see the path, e.g. via a variable)
```

A second route, for both mechanisms: neither `bwrap` nor `unshare` is given a new PID namespace or a fresh `/proc` (`--dev-bind / /` keeps the host's `/proc`), so `/proc/<pid>/root/<root>/…` of any same-user process outside the sandbox (the Kyvor host itself) resolves in the host's mount namespace, where no tmpfs hides the store. [INFERENCE] Whether the kernel allows that `/proc/<pid>/root` traversal depends on the ptrace access check for same-uid processes; not run.

## Expected
`crates/kyvor-base/src/confine.rs:7-10` and `docs/user/roles.md:157-165`: hidden directories are out of the child's reach; nothing runs unconfined.

## Steps to reproduce
Not run (no Linux machine or container available). From the code:
1. Linux with unprivileged user namespaces and no `bwrap` on `PATH`.
2. Workflow mode on with a private case stored.
3. A bash call running `umount "$H/work"; cat "$H/work/…/holdout/<case>"` with `H` set to the Kyvor home.
Reproduced on the latest attempt: not tried.

## Evidence
`crates/kyvor-base/src/confine.rs:48` and `:138-152`:
```rust
const UNSHARE_SCRIPT: &str = r#"n=$1; shift; while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do mount -t tmpfs none "$1" || exit 126; shift; n=$((n - 1)); done; exec "$@""#;
...
"--user".into(), "--map-root-user".into(), "--mount".into(), "--".into(), "/bin/sh".into(), "-c".into(), UNSHARE_SCRIPT.into(),
```
The script `exec`s the command with every capability the mapped root has in its own user namespace; nothing drops them or locks the mounts. The bwrap branch (`:124-137`) uses `--dev-bind / /` without `--unshare-pid` or `--proc /proc`.

## Likely cause
`UNSHARE_SCRIPT` keeps the command as namespace root with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` over mounts it created itself, so the hiding mounts are removable; and neither mechanism replaces `/proc`. [INFERENCE] from the code and Linux namespace semantics.

## Proposed fix
For `unshare`: after mounting, drop to a non-root uid and capabilities before `exec` (e.g. `setpriv --reuid=<uid> --regid=<gid> --init-groups --inh-caps=-all --bounding-set=-all`), or nest a second user namespace (`unshare --user` again inside, so the tmpfs mounts become locked from the inner namespace's view), or require `bwrap` and refuse otherwise. For both: add `--unshare-pid --proc /proc` to bwrap and `--pid --fork --mount-proc` to unshare so `/proc` shows only the sandbox's processes.

Test (Linux-only, skipped when the mechanism is unavailable, next to `crates/kyvor-tools-shell/tests/tools/bash/confine.rs`): with a hidden root, a confined `umount <root>; cat <root>/case` and a confined `cat /proc/<parent pid>/root/<root>/case` both fail to print the case text.

## Environment
- Kyvor: built from source, master `35fe1379`
- OS: Darwin 25.5.0 (macOS, aarch64) for the reading; the Linux paths were not run
- Provider / model: anthropic-claude-code/claude-opus-5-5

items.title: Per-run sandbox for the local execution shell (hide host argv without killing background processes)
items.body:
Follow-up to #208.

#208 runs the local runtime's execution Bash under `bwrap` (`local_runtime._confined_argv`) with the read deny-set masked and `--unshare-user`, which refuses `/proc/<worker>/environ`. It deliberately does NOT use `--unshare-pid`: one sandbox per Bash call means a PID namespace kills every `cmd &` when the call returns (measured: a server started in one call answered `000` to the next).

Remaining gap: the confined shell sees every host process's **argv** via `ps`/`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. Not a regression (the shell was unconfined before), and Otto keeps credentials off argv by design, but any third-party process passing a token on its command line is readable.

Proposal: one persistent sandbox per RUN (shared PID + mount namespace that outlives individual Bash calls, e.g. a long-lived `bwrap --unshare-pid` init that each call `nsenter`s / execs into), torn down in `run_json`'s `finally` and by `kill_tree` on abort/timeout.

Notes:
- `bwrap --proc` takes no mount options, so `hidepid=2` is not available that way.
- Must keep `test_a_background_process_outlives_its_call` green and add an argv-canary test (another process's argv invisible).

items.body:
### What version of Codex is running?

`codex-cli 0.144.1`

### What platform is affected?

- Unraid Linux
- Kernel: `6.12.54-Unraid`
- Architecture: `x86_64`
- Sandbox policy: `workspace-write`
- Workspace filesystem: ZFS
- Root filesystem: the initial `rootfs`

```text
$ findmnt -no TARGET,FSTYPE,PROPAGATION,OPTIONS /
/ rootfs private rw,size=31643352k,nr_inodes=7910838,inode64

$ findmnt -T /mnt/cache/projects/<repo> -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
TARGET                     SOURCE         FSTYPE OPTIONS
/mnt/cache/projects        cache/projects zfs    rw,relatime,xattr,posixacl,casesensitive
```

There is no system `bwrap` on this host, so Codex uses its bundled bubblewrap helper.

### What issue are you seeing?

Every sandboxed command fails before the requested command executes:

```text
bwrap: pivot_root: Invalid argument
```

This affects harmless read-only commands such as `pwd`, `git status --short`, and `rg --files`.

Because the sandbox bootstrap fails, the only available retry path is execution outside the sandbox. With an approval-based policy, this makes ordinary repository inspection appear to require approval for every command.

The same commands succeed normally when executed outside the Codex sandbox, confirming that repository ownership and workspace permissions are not the problem.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run Codex 0.144.1 on an Unraid host where `/` remains mounted as the kernel's initial `rootfs`.
2. Start a session using the default bubblewrap filesystem sandbox and `workspace-write`.
3. Ask Codex to run any command, for example:

   ```sh
   pwd
   ```

4. Observe:

   ```text
   bwrap: pivot_root: Invalid argument
   ```

5. Retry the same command outside the sandbox and observe that it succeeds.

### Additional diagnostics

Unprivileged user and mount namespaces are available. Both of these complete successfully:

```sh
unshare --user --map-root-user true
unshare --user --map-root-user --mount true
```

The namespace limit is also nonzero:

```text
$ cat /proc/sys/user/max_user_namespaces
246490
```

This rules out the common case where unprivileged user namespaces are disabled.

The legacy Landlock fallback is present but does not work on this host:

```sh
codex --enable use_legacy_landlock sandbox linux /bin/true
```

Result:

```text
thread 'main' panicked at linux-sandbox/src/linux_run_main.rs:252:9:
error applying legacy Linux sandbox restrictions: Sandbox(LandlockRestrict)
```

### Likely cause

Linux documents `EINVAL` from `pivot_root(2)` when “the current root is on the rootfs (initial ramfs) mount”:

https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pivot_root.2.html

That exactly matches both the error and this host's mount topology.

### Expected behavior

Codex should either:

1. support sandboxing when the host root is the initial `rootfs` without relying on an unsupported `pivot_root()` operation;
2. detect this mount topology at startup and use a compatible sandbox backend; or
3. surface a clear compatibility diagnostic rather than failing every command and causing repeated approval escalations.

This appears distinct from AppArmor/user-namespace failures because namespace creation succeeds and the syscall fails specifically at `pivot_root`.

items.title: Fix heap buffer overflow in FixedStringReducer for fixed-width string columns
items.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Internal security finding sfind-80a08805e3754ecd8750a7c1fa474dc9.

#### What does this implement or fix?

`FixedStringReducer` wrote past its destination buffer for fixed-width string columns.

`get_fixed_string_reducer` sized the output with `check_all=false`, so for a non-compacted slice only the *first*
non-null string's length was measured (`get_first_string_size`). The destination buffer is `row_count * alloc_width`,
while `FixedStringReducer::reduce` `memcpy`s each string's full `sv.size()` into a `column_width_`-sized slot. Both the
string pool and the string offsets are decoded from the segment body, so a writer of the segment controls the contents
and lengths — any string longer than the first one overflows the heap buffer for every such row. The equal-length
invariant of a fixed-width column is enforced only by well-behaved writers, never by the reader.

Changes:

- `get_max_string_size_in_column` now always measures every string in the column; the `check_all` parameter and the
  first-string-only path are gone, so the unsafe sizing path no longer exists.
- `FixedStringReducer::reduce` raises `E_ASSERTION_FAILURE` if a string is wider than the allocated slot, as
  defence in depth against any future path that under-sizes the buffer.
- New test `FixedStringReducer.CraftedPoolWithVaryingStringLengths` builds a non-compacted fixed-width string column
  whose pool holds a 1-byte first string and 16-byte later strings, runs the pandas reduce path, and asserts the output
  is sized from the longest string and null-padded.

No API, on-disk format, or behaviour change for well-formed data: for a fixed-width column written by ArcticDB all
strings in a slice have the same length, so the measured width is unchanged. Reads of previously undetected malformed
segments now allocate the correct width instead of overflowing.

#### Any other comments?

## Validation

All lines below were produced by actually executing the PoC and tests in this environment.

Build: `cmake -DTEST=ON -DARCTICDB_USING_ADDRESS_SANITIZER=ON --preset linux-debug cpp` plus
`cmake --build cpp/out/linux-debug-build --target test_unit_arcticdb` (gcc 11.4, AddressSanitizer).

```

```

The fourth runtime line (`RUNTIME VALIDATION [SKIPPED]`) does not apply — no validation step had to be skipped.

items.title: Mounting 2nd device of multi-device root btrfs via udisks/Dolphin stacks it on `/`, breaking user namespaces (Flatpak/Steam/rpm-ostreed)
items.body:
## Environment
- Bazzite: 44.20260608.0 (bazzite-nvidia-open, Kinoite)
- Kernel: 7.0.9-ogc3.2.fc44.x86_64 (Open Gaming Collective kernel)
- NVIDIA driver: 610.43.02
- systemd: 257.x

## What happened
After a reboot (triggered manually, without KDE session restore for Steam/Chrome),
the following applications failed to start:
- Steam (native): "Steam now requires user namespaces to be enabled"
- Google Chrome (Flatpak): bwrap namespace error
- Heroic Games Launcher (Flatpak): bwrap namespace error

Lutris (native RPM) continued to work. Applications that were in KDE session
restore on previous boots worked fine.

## Root cause
`systemd-nsresourced.service` attaches BPF-LSM programs at boot
(`userns_restrict_*`) that restrict unprivileged user namespace creation.

On the **standard Fedora kernel**, these BPF programs appear to operate
permissively and do not actually block namespace creation. On the **OGC kernel**
(`ogc3.2`), they enforce restrictions, blocking `bwrap` calls from Steam,
Flatpak, and other sandboxed applications.

This was confirmed by:
```
$ unshare --user echo "OK"
unshare: unshare failed: Operation not permitted
```
After masking `systemd-nsresourced.socket` and rebooting:
```
$ unshare --user echo "OK"
OK
```

## Why it doesn't manifest consistently
Applications launched via **KDE session restore** succeed because they start
within a ~20-30s race window before BPF programs become fully enforcing.
Applications launched manually after full boot initialization are blocked.

The issue became visible due to a Steam client update (1781041600 → 1782257239,
June 24 2026) that made bubblewrap sandboxing mandatory with no fallback.

## Workaround
```bash
sudo systemctl mask systemd-nsresourced.socket
sudo systemctl stop systemd-nsresourced
# reboot required to unload BPF hooks
```

## Similar reports
- linux-hardened kernel (Arch Linux) exhibits the same behavior:
  https://bbs.archlinux.org/viewtopic.php?id=297658
- `bubblewrap-suid` is not available in Fedora 44 repos as an alternative fix

## Suggested fix
Either:
1. Mask `systemd-nsresourced.socket` in the Bazzite base image, or
2. Investigate why OGC kernel's BPF-LSM enforces nsresourced restrictions
   while standard Fedora kernel does not, and align behavior

items.title: Studio: let the Linux tool sandbox use bubblewrap on NixOS and in FHS launchers
items.body:
Fixes #13688.

## Problem

On NixOS, tool calls never get bubblewrap isolation, and Studio says bubblewrap is not installed even though it is. `_trusted_bwrap_path()` refuses bwrap in two cases:

- **A Nix-installed bwrap.** `/nix/store` is `root:nixbld 1775`, and any group-writable ancestor is refused.
- **Desktop's FHS env.** The nixpkgs package and `appimageTools` both run Desktop inside a `buildFHSEnv`. There, host-root files show as uid 65534 and `/` is owned by the user.

Once bwrap was accepted, the sandbox still failed. In the FHS env, Studio's Python loader and `/usr/bin` are symlinks into `/nix/store`, which was not mounted in the jail. On plain NixOS, the Terminal tool's PATH, `/run/current-system/sw/bin`, is missing from the jail.

## Fix

- Accept a root-owned sticky directory as an ancestor. Other writers cannot rename or delete root's entries in it.
- Add `UNSLOTH_BWRAP_PATH` to pin bubblewrap. The file must not be writable by group or others, and must be owned by root, or by the overflow uid inside a user namespace. Ancestors are not checked.
- In a user namespace, if a pin would fix the refusal, the message says so instead of offering an install.
- Mount `/nix/store` in the jail when the interpreter or the host's `true` resolves into it, and link `/run/current-system` to its target.

## Boundaries

- A bwrap the Studio user owns or can write is always refused.
- A pin skips the ancestor checks, and only a pin can make the overflow uid trusted. Whoever sets Studio's environment already controls what it runs.
- Hosts without `/nix/store` get the same jail as before.
- #13164 edits the same ancestor loop, so the two will conflict.

## Verification

New tests are in `test_sandbox_linux.py`, `test_sandbox_setup_plan.py` and `test_sandbox_install_remediation.py`. The sandbox, permission and tool-policy suites pass, except `test_confinement_survives_nested_processes`. It fails on main too, because it matches the English "Permission denied" message.

I compared main with this branch using the real live probe. Python and bash payloads tried to write to `$HOME`:

| Setup | main | branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NixOS VM, system bwrap | refused | isolated, `$HOME` read-only |
| NixOS VM, `buildFHSEnv` with Studio's uv Python, no pin | refused | refused, message names the pin |
| Same, pinned | refused | isolated, `$HOME` read-only |
| Ubuntu, real Studio under `unshare --user --map-current-user`, pinned | "bubblewrap is not installed." | isolated |
| Plain Ubuntu | isolated | isolated |

On the branch, a user-owned bwrap is still refused, whether it comes first on PATH or is pinned. Disabling either jail change brings back its failure.

Not tested: Flatpak, rootless containers, the AppImage binary itself, and nix-ld.

items.title: Linux: option for a read-only /proc/sys inside the sandbox (in bwrap's /proc and in apply-seccomp's own /proc)
items.body:
## Use case

We run MCP servers through `SandboxManager.wrapWithSandbox` from a long-running systemd service, as a non-root user with `NoNewPrivileges=yes`. We want the service unit's `ProtectKernelTunables=yes`, which makes `/proc/sys` (and some other `/proc` paths) read-only. With it on, the sandboxed servers no longer start on Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.17.0-1022-azure, systemd 255). We ran bwrap as the service's user in a transient unit, with the arguments sandbox-runtime gives it (`--ro-bind / / --dev /dev --unshare-pid --unshare-user --cap-drop ALL --proc /proc`). It printed:

```
ProtectKernelTunables=yes:  bwrap: Can't mount proc on /newroot/proc: Operation not permitted
ProtectControlGroups=yes:   started
neither:                    started
```

Our understanding: the unit's read-only bind mounts over parts of `/proc` mean the existing procfs is no longer "fully visible", so the kernel refuses a new procfs mount in an unprivileged user namespace.

So the read-only `/proc/sys` has to come from inside the sandbox instead. We found no way to get one today.

## What we measured

Versions: `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime` 0.0.78 and bubblewrap 0.9.0, on Ubuntu 24.04 in CI (kernel 6.17.0-1022-azure, systemd 255) and on a local Linux 6.18. Items 2 and 3 were measured locally.

1. **Where `/proc` is mounted.** In `dist/sandbox/linux-sandbox-utils.js`:
   - the filesystem rules are pushed at line 2515 (`bwrapArgs.push(...fsArgs)`);
   - then `--dev /dev` (2518), `--unshare-pid` (2526), and `--unshare-user` with `--cap-drop ALL`;
   - then `--proc /proc` (2546).

   Every config rule (`filesystem.denyRead`, `allowWrite`, `denyWrite`) goes before the fresh `/proc`, and the rules skip `/proc` anyway. So no config option can make anything under `/proc` read-only.

2. **A bind placed after bwrap's `--proc` is hidden.** As an experiment we inserted `--ro-bind /proc/sys /proc/sys` right after `--proc /proc` in the wrapped command. bwrap applies it. Then the seccomp helper (`vendor/seccomp/*/apply-seccomp`, whose strings include `apply-seccomp: mount(/proc)`) unshares PID and mount namespaces and mounts another fresh `/proc` on top. Inside the sandbox, `/proc/self/mountinfo` shows, in order:
   - the `/proc` from `--ro-bind / /` (ro);
   - bwrap's `/proc` (rw);
   - our `/proc/sys` bind (ro), on bwrap's `/proc`;
   - the helper's `/proc` (rw), stacked on bwrap's `/proc` and hiding the bind.

   `stat -c %m /proc/sys` reports `/proc`, so the visible `/proc/sys` is the helper's, and it isn't read-only. Skipping the helper (`allowAllUnixSockets`) would drop the unix-socket block, which we want to keep.

3. **What holds today.** The caller is non-root, so the sandboxed process has no capabilities, and writes to `/proc/sys/*` fail with EACCES from file permissions. `/sys/fs/cgroup` is already read-only inside, through `--ro-bind / /`. A read-only `/proc/sys` would add defense in depth: a privilege escalation inside the sandbox would still face a read-only mount.

## Proposed option

A Linux config option, for example `filesystem.readOnlyProcSys: true`, or a general `readOnlyProcPaths: string[]`. When set:
- bwrap gets `--remount-ro /proc/sys` (or an equivalent read-only bind of the fresh `/proc`'s own `sys`) right after `--proc /proc`;
- `apply-seccomp` does the same after its own `mount(/proc)`: bind `/proc/sys` onto itself and remount it read-only, before it drops privileges and applies the filter.

The visible `/proc/sys` is then read-only both with and without the seccomp helper. Callers in hardened service managers get the effect of `ProtectKernelTunables` without that directive breaking bubblewrap's `/proc` mount.

If an upstream fix for the interaction between `ProtectKernelTunables` and bubblewrap is preferable (for example a documented supported configuration), we'd welcome that too. We're happy to test either in our CI.

items.title: Sandbox fails under Termux + proot Debian: cannot establish app-server socket mount isolation

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary

Codex CLI 0.156.0 cannot initialize the default Linux filesystem sandbox inside Termux + proot-distro Debian on Android.

The minimal direct sandbox command:

```bash
codex sandbox linux -- /bin/pwd
```

fails immediately with:

```text
error building bubblewrap command: cannot establish app-server socket mount isolation
```

The same error occurs for ordinary read-only commands in the TUI when using the normal restricted/workspace-write sandbox. If the command is explicitly approved to run outside the sandbox, it succeeds.

## Environment

- Codex CLI: `0.156.0`
- Install: standalone ARM64 Linux build
- Architecture: `aarch64`
- Userspace: Debian 13 (trixie) under Termux `proot-distro`
- Kernel string exposed through proot:
  ```text
  Linux version 6.17.0-PRoot-Distro (proot@termux)
  ```
- Bubblewrap: `0.12.0`
- util-linux / unshare: `2.41.5`
- Python: `3.13.13`
- Codex auth: ChatGPT
- Approval policy: `on-request`
- Filesystem sandbox: restricted / workspace-write
- Network sandbox: restricted

`codex doctor --json` reports the install, auth, Git, provider reachability, WebSocket connectivity, state databases, and sandbox helper configuration as OK. The only overall warning is terminal width (63 columns).

## Minimal reproduction

From a Git repository inside the Debian proot environment:

```bash
codex sandbox linux -- /bin/pwd
```

### Actual result

```text
error building bubblewrap command: cannot establish app-server socket mount isolation
```

### Expected result

The command should execute under the normal restricted Linux sandbox and print the current working directory.

## TUI reproduction

Start Codex normally with the default restricted/workspace-write sandbox and ask it to run a read-only command such as:

```bash
pwd
```

The first sandboxed attempt fails before command execution:

```text
error building bubblewrap command: cannot establish app-server socket mount isolation
```

Codex then asks for approval to run the command outside the sandbox. If approved, the command succeeds.

This reproduces for `pwd`, `ls -la`, `git status --short`, bundled `rg --files`, and `python3 --version`.

## Diagnostics

### Namespace support

Both of these succeed with exit code 0:

```bash
unshare --user --map-root-user /bin/true
unshare --mount /bin/true
```

### Filesystem/runtime operations outside the Codex sandbox

All of the following work in the proot environment:

- read `/proc/version`
- resolve `/proc/self/exe`
- create/delete files in `/tmp`
- symlink round trip
- chmod + execute a temporary script
- advisory file locks
- Unix domain sockets
- localhost TCP sockets
- shell subprocess spawning
- Git fetch/pull/push

### Bubblewrap package

```text
bubblewrap 0.12.0
unshare from util-linux 2.41.5
```

A manual bubblewrap test still fails in this proot environment:

```bash
bwrap \
  --unshare-user \
  --unshare-ipc \
  --ro-bind / / \
  /bin/sh -c 'pwd; echo sandbox-ok'
```

Result:

```text
bwrap: Creating proc failed: File exists
```

The same failure occurs with `--unshare-pid` included.

### proot path leakage visible from processes

Inside Debian, Python reports:

```text
system=Android
machine=aarch64
```

and:

```text
/proc/self/exe -> /data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/python3.13
```

So the Debian userspace is running over the underlying Termux/Android mount/proc view.

## Related issue

This appears related to #30153, which also reports Codex sandbox initialization failure under Termux + proot Debian, but the failure mode is different.

- #30153 (Codex 0.142.2): `bwrap: fchdir to oldroot: No such file or directory`
- This report (Codex 0.156.0): `cannot establish app-server socket mount isolation`

The current error is emitted even by the dedicated `codex sandbox linux -- /bin/pwd` command.

## Impact

The CLI is otherwise usable on Android through Termux + proot Debian, including ChatGPT authentication, Git/GitHub operations, editing, Python execution, sockets, and subprocesses.

However, the normal restricted sandbox cannot start. The practical choices are currently:

1. approve each fallback execution outside the sandbox, or
2. use full access, which removes the safety boundary.

For users intentionally avoiding full access, this makes the Android/proot workflow much less practical.

## Additional observation

The exact error string appears in `codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/daemon_mounts.rs`, where Codex validates mount aliases for the app-server socket directory using `/proc/self/mountinfo`.

Given proot's synthetic filesystem view and the underlying Android/Termux mount table, this may be a compatibility issue in that mount-isolation validation path rather than a missing namespace capability.

items.title: Allow --uid and --gid without --unshare-user when running as root
items.body: When root, it's not necessary to --unshare-user to be able to change uid/gid, so bubblewrap shouldn't require it.

items.title: Don't implicily enable --unshare-user when not running as root
items.body: If already in a user namespace, a regular user can have all the required permissions necessary for bubblewrap to function correctly. Hence bubblewrap shouldn't implicitly enable --unshare-user when not running as root if the user has all the required capabilities for bubblewrap to function correctly.

items.title: --unshare-user doesn't work when procfs mounted with hidepid=1
items.body:
I've received this bug report in Debian: <https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=867847>. The rest of this issue report is quoting Guilhem Moulin.

---

I noticed that bubblewrap refuses to create a new user namespace when
the procfs is mounted (outside the container) with hidepid≥1.

    $ sudo mount -o remount,rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,hidepid=0 /proc
    $ bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user true; echo $?
    0
    $ sudo mount -o remount,rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,hidepid=1 /proc
    $ bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user true; echo $?
    setting up uid map: Operation not permitted
    1

It doesn't help to also create a new PID namespace:

    $ bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-pid --proc /proc true; echo $?
    setting up uid map: Operation not permitted
    1

Not sure if that's the intended behavior or not.  (In any case, it's not
documented.)  But when a new PID namespace is also created and /proc is
remounted, couldn't bwrap set hidepid=0 in the container?

Moreover, although the children do terminate, the bwrap processes do not
(and sending SIGTERM is not enough to terminate them):

    $ sudo ps -eo pid,args | grep bwrap
    13475 bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user true
    13489 bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-user --unshare-pid --proc /proc true

And the leftover container's effective and saved set UIds are still 0:

    $ sudo egrep '^([UG]id|Groups):' /proc/13475/status
    Uid:	1000	0	0	1000
    Gid:	1000	1000	1000	1000
    Groups:	20 24 25 27 29 30 44 46 108 118 119 128 1000

items.title: fix(workflow): default MLflowRecorder.load_object to restricted unpickler
items.body:
## Description
`MLflowRecorder.load_object` defaulted to `pickle.Unpickler`, so every artifact downloaded from the MLflow tracking server (reached via `RecordTemp.load`, `R.load_object`, `OnlineStrategy`, `RecorderCollector`, updaters, ...) was deserialized with an unrestricted unpickler. A crafted artifact on a shared/remote tracking server executes arbitrary code on load.

Change:
```diff
-    def load_object(self, name, unpickler=pickle.Unpickler):
+    def load_object(self, name, unpickler=RestrictedUnpickler):
```
`RestrictedUnpickler` (`qlib.utils.pickle_utils`, already used for file/DB/Mongo deserialization elsewhere in qlib) only allows `pandas`/`numpy` and the explicit whitelist. The `unpickler` kwarg is kept, so callers who intentionally load arbitrary model checkpoints from a trusted store can still pass `pickle.Unpickler` explicitly, or extend the whitelist via `add_safe_class`.

Added `tests/misc/test_recorder_load_object.py` covering a benign DataFrame round-trip and a rejected `__reduce__` gadget (mocked `MlflowClient`, no server needed).

Finding: `sfind-d9006971e89c45bf87156f41cd4a3cca`.

## Motivation and Context
Remote MLflow artifacts must be treated as untrusted input; unrestricted `pickle` deserialization is RCE.

## How Has This Been Tested?
- [ ] Pass the test by running: `pytest qlib/tests/test_all_pipeline.py` under upper directory of `qlib`. (requires downloaded market data; not run in this environment)
- [x] If you are adding a new feature, test on your own test scripts.

## Validation
Sandbox setup (throwaway temp dir, unprivileged user namespace with no network egress, file-based MLflow store, harmless `PWNED` marker file as payload effect; no real credentials read):
```
SANDBOX=$(mktemp -d /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox.XXXXXX)        # -> /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox.dm7BCD (pre-fix)
                                                            #    /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox_post.vJedAD (post-fix)
unshare --map-root-user --net -- env MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE=true PYTHONPATH=/home/ubuntu/repos/qlib python /tmp/poc.py "$SANDBOX"
```
The PoC logs a pickle whose `__reduce__` returns `(os.system, ("echo pwned > $SANDBOX/PWNED",))` as an MLflow artifact and then calls `MLflowRecorder.load_object("evil.pkl")`.

```
RUNTIME VALIDATION [PRE-FIX]: EXPLOIT SUCCEEDED - reduce gadget (os.system) executed during MLflowRecorder.load_object; marker file /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox.dm7BCD/PWNED was created
RUNTIME VALIDATION [POST-FIX]: EXPLOIT BLOCKED - RestrictedUnpickler rejected forbidden class os.system; no marker file created, load_object raised UnpicklingError
RUNTIME VALIDATION [REGRESSION]: tests/misc (incl. new test_recorder_load_object.py) 13 passed, 0 failed; tests/test_workflow.py 1 passed, 0 failed
SANDBOX VALIDATION: unshare user+net namespace (unshare --map-root-user --net) in /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox.dm7BCD (pre) / /tmp/qlib_pwn_sandbox_post.vJedAD (post) - payload effect observed pre-fix: yes, post-fix: no
```
Post-fix `load_object` raised `LoadObjectError: Forbidden class: posix.system. Only whitelisted classes are allowed for security reasons.`

## Screenshots of Test Results (if appropriate):
1. Pipeline test: not run (needs market data download)
2. Your own tests: `python -m pytest tests/misc -q` -> `13 passed`

## Types of changes
- [x] Fix bugs
- [ ] Add new feature
- [ ] Update documentation
